title: Inside a stem: two sets of pipes, growth rings and tissues

summary.text: Most of a tree trunk is made of dead cells, yet the tree is alive. Take away one thin strip of bark all the way round the trunk, and the whole tree slowly dies. Why? Most plants have two sets of pipes. Xylem pipes are dead and hollow, and they carry water up from the roots. Phloem pipes are alive, and they carry sugar from the leaves to every part that needs food. In a tree the phloem lies just under the bark, and a thin layer called the cambium adds new wood every year, which makes the growth rings. Your child maps these pipes with dye in a root, a stem and a leaf stalk, reads a tree's rings, and learns how skin, packing and pipes work together as tissues.
summary.art: A cut tree stump showing rings, with a thin green living layer under the bark drawn brighter than the pale wood inside, and a small cut stem with coloured dots beside it.

intro.hook: Peel a banana slowly. Long pale strings stay stuck to the fruit. They run from the stalk end to the tip. What are these strings for?
intro.text: Look for the same kind of string in a leaf stalk and on a peeled orange. In the first activity, String Hunt, you pull them out and compare them. Then, in Pipe Maps, you use coloured water to test what at least some of the strings do.
intro.art: A half-peeled banana with pale strings running along the fruit from the stalk end, and a child's fingers pulling one string away.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a tissue is, and name a plant's three kinds: skin, packing and transport.
By the end I can tell xylem from phloem: what each carries, which way, and whether its cells are alive.
By the end I can show where the pipes sit in a root, a stem and a leaf stalk, and say why.
By the end I can explain 'source to sink', and why food in the phloem can travel up or down.
By the end I can explain how a trunk gets thicker, and why losing a ring of bark kills a tree.
By the end I can read growth rings, and say when rings can mislead us.
By the end I can plan a fair test with dye, and give my claim, evidence and reasoning.
By the end I can say which parts of a tree are living and which are dead, and what the dead cells do.

terms.meaning: A cell is the smallest living unit of a body. Every plant and animal is built from cells. A plant cell has a stiff wall around the outside.
terms.example: One thin slice of onion skin is a sheet of hundreds of cells, each like a tiny room.
terms.art: A sheet of box-shaped plant cells, each with a wall, drawn like a tiled floor.

terms.meaning: A tissue is a group of cells of the same kind that do one job together.
terms.example: The see-through skin you can peel from a leaf is a tissue. So is the bundle of pipes in a banana string.
terms.art: Many similar cells joined in a sheet, with a bracket and the word 'tissue'.

terms.meaning: The epidermis is the skin tissue of a plant. It is usually one cell thick. It keeps water in and germs out.
terms.example: The shiny surface of a mango leaf is the epidermis, covered with a thin layer of wax.
terms.art: A cut leaf seen from the side, with the single top row of cells coloured in.

terms.meaning: Ground tissue fills the space between the skin and the pipes. Its cells store food, make food in green parts, and help hold the plant up.
terms.example: The soft flesh of a potato is ground tissue packed with stored starch.
terms.art: A cut stem with the pale filling between the skin and the pipe dots shaded.

terms.meaning: Vascular tissue is the transport tissue of a plant. It is made of two kinds of pipes, xylem and phloem.
terms.example: The veins of a leaf are vascular tissue. So are the strings on a peeled banana.
terms.art: A leaf with its veins drawn in two colours side by side, blue and gold.

terms.meaning: A vascular bundle is a strand of xylem and phloem pipes running side by side, often with strong fibres round them.
terms.example: Each coloured dot you see when you cut a dyed stem across is one vascular bundle.
terms.art: One dot from a cut stem drawn large, showing wide blue pipes on one side and small gold pipes on the other.

terms.meaning: Xylem is the tissue that carries water and dissolved minerals up from the roots. Its pipes are made of dead, hollow cells with hard walls.
terms.example: The wood of a teak door is old xylem.
terms.art: A stack of hollow cells with no end walls, with blue arrows pointing up through them.

terms.meaning: A vessel is one long xylem pipe. It forms when a column of cells die and their end walls break down, so the cells join into one tube.
terms.example: The tiny holes you can see on the cut end of a piece of teak are vessels.
terms.art: A long hollow tube built of short cell sections joined end to end, with spiral thickening on the wall.

terms.meaning: Lignin is a hard, waterproof substance that plants add to some cell walls. It makes wood stiff.
terms.example: A coconut shell is very hard because the walls of its cells are full of lignin.
terms.art: A cell wall drawn thick and dark, beside a thin pale wall, with a small coconut shell.

terms.meaning: Phloem is the tissue that carries sugar from where it is made or stored to where it is needed. Its pipes are made of living cells.
terms.example: The sweet neera that drips from a cut coconut flower stalk is phloem sap.
terms.art: A column of living cells with sieve-like end walls, with gold arrows pointing both up and down.

terms.meaning: A sieve tube is one phloem pipe. It is a line of living cells. The wall between two cells has many holes, like a tea strainer, so sap can pass.
terms.example: An aphid pushes her mouth tube into one single sieve tube to feed.
terms.art: Two long cells joined end to end, with a round plate full of holes between them.

terms.meaning: A companion cell is a small living cell beside each sieve tube cell. The companion cell keeps the sieve tube cell alive, because the sieve tube cell has no nucleus.
terms.example: Each sieve tube cell in a mango twig has a companion cell alongside.
terms.art: A wide sieve tube cell with a small cell alongside, joined by tiny channels, the small cell showing a nucleus.

terms.meaning: Sap is the liquid that moves inside a plant's pipes. Xylem sap is mostly water with minerals. Phloem sap is water with a lot of sugar.
terms.example: Sugarcane juice is sweet because phloem sap delivered sugar to the stem, where it is stored.
terms.art: Two drops side by side, one clear and labelled 'xylem sap', one golden and labelled 'phloem sap'.

terms.meaning: A source is a part of a plant that gives sugar to the phloem. It either makes the sugar or lets go of stored food.
terms.example: A mango leaf in sunlight is a source. A sprouting potato is a source too.
terms.art: A green leaf in sunlight with gold dots leaving along its stalk.

terms.meaning: A sink is a part of a plant that takes sugar from the phloem, to use or to store.
terms.example: A swelling mango fruit, a growing root tip and a new leaf bud are all sinks.
terms.art: A growing fruit and a root tip with gold dots arriving at each.

terms.meaning: Translocation is the movement of sugar and other food through the phloem, from sources to sinks.
terms.example: At night, sugar made in a tapioca leaf during the day is translocated down to the fat roots.
terms.art: A whole plant with gold arrows running from the leaves to the fruit, the tips and the roots.

terms.meaning: A meristem is a place in a plant where cells keep dividing to make new cells. Plants grow only from their meristems.
terms.example: The very tip of a money plant shoot is a meristem. New leaves come from there.
terms.art: A shoot tip and a root tip, each with a small glowing dome of tiny cells.

terms.meaning: The cambium is a meristem shaped like a thin sleeve between the wood and the bark. It adds new xylem on the inside and new phloem on the outside.
terms.example: When you peel fresh bark off a twig, the wet, slippery surface is where the cambium was.
terms.art: A cut trunk with a thin bright green circle between the wood and the bark, and arrows pointing inward and outward from it.

terms.meaning: Wood is xylem that the cambium has made, year after year. Most of its cells are dead.
terms.example: A rosewood chair, a pine packing crate and a neem twig are all wood.
terms.art: A cut log, with the whole area inside the bark shaded and labelled 'wood = xylem'.

terms.meaning: Bark is everything outside the cambium. The inner bark is living phloem. The outer bark is dead cork that protects the tree.
terms.example: The thick, cracked skin of a neem trunk is outer bark. Cinnamon sticks are dried inner bark.
terms.art: A slice of trunk edge showing two layers outside the wood: a pale inner layer and a rough outer layer.

terms.meaning: A growth ring is the layer of wood a tree adds in one growing season. Rings show up because wood made early in the season looks different from wood made late.
terms.example: Count the rings on a teak stump from the centre to the bark to learn about how many years the tree lived.
terms.art: A tree stump seen from above with clear light and dark rings.

terms.meaning: Sapwood is the pale outer wood whose pipes still carry water. Heartwood is the older, darker wood in the middle, whose pipes are blocked.
terms.example: In a cut rosewood log, the pale rim is sapwood and the dark purple-brown middle is heartwood.
terms.art: A cut log with a pale outer band and a dark centre, each labelled.

terms.meaning: Girdling means removing or squeezing the bark in a complete ring round a stem. It cuts the phloem, so sugar cannot pass.
terms.example: A wire tied tightly round a young tree and left for years can girdle the tree.
terms.art: A trunk with a ring of bark missing, swollen above the ring and thinner below.

terms.meaning: Dendrochronology is the science of working out dates and past weather from tree rings.
terms.example: Scientists in India have used the rings of old teak trees in Kerala to study monsoons of the past 500 years.
terms.art: A scientist holding a thin pencil-like core of wood marked with rings, beside a calendar.

explanations.concept: Tissues: cells that do one job together
explanations.definition: A tissue is a group of cells of the same kind doing one job together. A plant has three kinds of tissue: skin tissue on the outside, transport tissue that carries water and food, and ground tissue that fills the rest.
explanations.description: A plant is not one lump of the same stuff. Cut any stem across and you see different areas. The outside is a skin, called the epidermis. It is usually one cell thick, and it is covered in wax so the plant does not dry out. Inside are bundles of pipes, the vascular tissue. Everything else is ground tissue, which you can think of as packing. But the packing is busy. In a green stem, the packing cells make food. In a potato or a carrot, they store food. Some packing cells grow thick, hard walls and become fibres that hold the plant up. Why does a plant need tissues at all? A single cell can only do so much. A cell that is a good pipe is a bad store, and a cell that is a good skin is a bad pipe. So cells take different jobs and depend on each other, the way the people in a town do.
examples: The waxy skin of a brinjal is epidermis, the flesh is ground tissue, and the faint lines running through the flesh are vascular bundles.
Jute fibre, grown in West Bengal and Assam, is bundles of strong fibre cells from the stem of the jute plant.
The gritty bits in a pear or a chikoo are tiny groups of cells with very thick, hard walls.
explanations.art: A cut stem drawn as a circle with three areas in three colours: a thin skin, a ring of pipe bundles, and packing filling the rest.

explanations.concept: Two sets of pipes in every vein
explanations.definition: Every vein of a plant holds two kinds of pipe side by side. Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves and stores to wherever food is needed.
explanations.description: In the Pipe Maps test, the dye showed up as dots. Each dot is a vascular bundle. The dye stains only the xylem, because xylem carries the water you gave. Right beside every dyed dot lies a patch of phloem that the dye does not show. In a stem, the phloem is on the side of the bundle nearer the skin, and the xylem is nearer the middle. Why two sets, and not one? Because the two loads travel in different directions and in different ways. Water goes one way, from root to leaf, and most of it then leaves the plant as vapour. Sugar starts in the leaves and must reach roots, fruits and buds, which may be above or below. One pipe could not do both jobs at once.
examples: The strings on a peeled banana are vascular bundles. They carried water and sugar into the growing fruit.
The white threads on a peeled orange are vascular bundles too.
A dried ridge gourd, sold as a loofah scrubber, is the tough net of vascular bundles and fibres left when the soft flesh has gone.
explanations.art: One vascular bundle drawn large, with wide blue-edged pipes labelled xylem on the inner side and small gold cells labelled phloem on the outer side.

explanations.concept: Xylem: pipes made of dead cells
explanations.definition: Xylem pipes are built from cells that have died and emptied. Their walls are hardened with lignin. Water is pulled up through them from the roots to the leaves.
explanations.description: A young xylem cell is alive. First the cell grows long. Then the cell builds a thick wall and stiffens the wall with lignin, often in rings or spirals. Then the cell breaks down everything inside, and dies. In a vessel, the end walls dissolve too, so a column of dead cells becomes one open tube. This death is not an accident. The cell's own genes switch it on at the right time. Why must the cell die? Because a living cell is full of jelly-like contents that would block the flow. Only an empty tube lets water through easily. The hard walls matter too. Water in the xylem is pulled from above, as you learned in the unit on how water climbs. A soft tube would be squashed flat by that pull, the way a paper straw flattens when you suck too hard. Lignin keeps the pipe open. The same hard walls hold the plant up, so xylem does two jobs: carrying and supporting.
examples: A wooden rolling pin is made of millions of dead xylem cells. They carried water once, and now they give the wood its strength.
Conifers such as deodar have narrower xylem cells, called tracheids, which pass water to each other through small pits in their side walls.
The spiral threads you sometimes see when you snap a lotus stem gently and pull the pieces apart are the wall thickenings of xylem cells.
explanations.art: Four drawings in a row showing one cell growing long, thickening the wall in spirals, emptying, and joining others into an open tube with blue water inside.

explanations.concept: Phloem: pipes made of living cells
explanations.definition: Phloem pipes are called sieve tubes. They are lines of living cells joined by end walls full of holes. They carry phloem sap, which is water with a lot of sugar dissolved in it.
explanations.description: Phloem cells stay alive, but they change a great deal. A sieve tube cell gets rid of the nucleus and most other inner parts, so that sap can flow through. A cell with no nucleus cannot keep going alone for long. So each sieve tube cell has a partner alongside, a companion cell, which makes what both cells need. Phloem sap is as sweet as a soft drink, or sweeter. Often between a tenth and a quarter of it is sugar. The sugar is mostly sucrose, the same sugar as in your kitchen. The sap also carries building materials for proteins, and signals from one part of the plant to another. Why must these cells stay alive when xylem cells die? Because loading sugar into the pipe and taking it out again is work that only a living cell membrane can do. Phloem sap moves more slowly than water in the xylem, usually about half a metre to one metre in an hour. This is simplified. Phloem tissue also holds fibre cells and storage cells, not only sieve tubes.
examples: Neera and toddy are phloem sap tapped from the cut flower stalks of coconut, palmyra and date palms. Palm jaggery is made by boiling this sap down.
Aphids, the tiny green or black insects on tender shoots of bean and hibiscus plants, feed on phloem sap.
Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a tree, and inner bark is phloem tissue.
explanations.art: A sieve tube drawn as long cells with strainer-like end plates, a small companion cell beside each, and gold sap flowing through the holes.

explanations.concept: From source to sink: which way the food goes
explanations.definition: Phloem sap flows from a source to a sink. A source is any part that puts sugar into the phloem. A sink is any part that takes sugar out. So the flow can be upward or downward, and it can change with the season.
explanations.description: Xylem has one direction, which is up. Phloem has no fixed direction. A leaf in the sun is a source. Roots, fruits, flowers and growing tips are sinks, because they cannot make enough food for themselves. So sugar from one mango leaf may go up to a fruit and down to the roots at the same time, through different sieve tubes. A part can also change sides. A young leaf is a sink while it grows, and becomes a source once it is big. A carrot root is a sink all through the first season, filling up with food. Next season the same root becomes a source, and sends food up to build the flower stalk. A potato does the same when it sprouts in a dark cupboard. There is no light there, so every bit of the new shoot is built from food that travels out of the potato. People once thought food sap only went down. It goes wherever the sinks are.
examples: When a mango tree is full of growing fruit, the fruit is the strongest sink, and the tree makes fewer new leaves.
A teak tree drops all their leaves in the dry season. The new leaves are built with food sent up from stores in the trunk and roots.
Tapioca farmers in Kerala and Tamil Nadu harvest the fat roots, which are sinks packed with starch.
explanations.art: A plant with gold arrows going from a sunny leaf up to a fruit and down to a root, and a second small picture of a sprouting potato with the arrow going from the potato up to the shoot.

explanations.concept: What pushes the phloem sap along?
explanations.description: The best explanation so far is called pressure flow. Ernst Münch, a German plant scientist, proposed it in 1930. At a source, cells load sugar into the sieve tubes. Water moves toward the place where it is held more tightly, and sugary sap holds water tightly, as you learned with osmosis. So water flows in from the xylem next door, and the pressure in the sieve tube rises. At a sink, cells take the sugar out, water leaves, and the pressure drops. Sap flows from high pressure to low pressure, the way toothpaste moves when you squeeze one end of the tube. The evidence is good. When an aphid's mouth tube is cut off while still stuck in a sieve tube, sap keeps oozing out of the cut end for hours, so the sap really is under pressure. In 2016, a team led by Michael Knoblauch measured pressures and pipe sizes in vines and tall trees and found they fit the idea. But the measurements are very hard to make, because a sieve tube seals itself the moment it is hurt. So scientists treat pressure flow as the leading idea, well supported, with details still being tested.
examples: Cut the tip off a full tube of toothpaste and squeeze the far end. The paste moves because the pressure is higher where you squeeze.
An aphid does not need to suck. The pressure in the sieve tube pushes sap into her.
Ants gather round aphids to drink honeydew, the sugary liquid that aphids pass out because they take in more sugar than they can use.

perspectives.who: Ernst Münch and most plant scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Sugar loading at the source draws water in and raises the pressure. The pressure difference between source and sink pushes the sap along.
In very tall trees the sieve tubes are long and narrow, and they asked whether pressure alone could push sap that far. Recent measurements suggest it can, but few trees have been measured.

explanations.art: A sieve tube drawn as a long tube, with sugar dots and water arrows entering at a leaf end marked 'high pressure' and leaving at a root end marked 'low pressure'.

explanations.concept: Where the pipes sit: centre, ring or arc
explanations.definition: In a root, the pipes are gathered in the centre. In the stem of most leafy plants, the bundles stand in a ring near the outside. In a leaf stalk, they lie in an arc.
explanations.description: The Pipe Maps test showed three different patterns. Why would one plant arrange the same pipes in three ways? Think about what each part has to bear. Xylem is the strongest tissue a young plant has, so where xylem sits decides where the part is strong. A root is pulled. When wind rocks the plant, the roots are tugged like ropes, and a rope is strongest with its strong strands together in the middle. A stem is bent. When a rod bends, the outside is stretched and squeezed the most, and the middle hardly at all. So strong material does the most good near the outside. That is why a hollow steel pipe makes a good cycle frame. A leaf stalk has to hold up a leaf blade and let it twist in the wind without snapping. An arc of bundles, like a gutter, does both. In grasses, palms, bananas and their relatives, the stem bundles are scattered all through the stem. This group of plants is called the monocots. The plants with a ring of bundles are mostly dicots. This reason is how engineers and botanists explain the patterns. It fits well, but the plant's history matters too.
examples: In a carrot, the paler core in the middle is xylem. That is where the dye appeared.
A cut piece of sugarcane shows bundles scattered all over the cut face as small dots. Sugarcane is a grass, and a monocot.
A celery stalk or a cauliflower leaf rib shows its bundles in a curved row. Each is a leaf stalk, not a stem.
explanations.art: Three cut faces side by side: a root with a star of pipes in the centre, a stem with a ring of bundles near the edge, and a C-shaped leaf stalk with an arc of bundles.

explanations.concept: Meristems: where a plant makes new cells
explanations.definition: A meristem is a region where cells keep dividing. A plant grows longer from meristems at the tips of shoots and roots. A plant grows thicker from a meristem inside the stem, called the cambium.
explanations.description: A grown plant cell is boxed in by a stiff wall and usually stops dividing. So a plant keeps special groups of small, thin-walled cells that stay young and go on dividing. These are the meristems. The ones at the tips make shoots and roots longer. This explains a famous puzzle. If you hammer a nail into a tree trunk one metre above the ground, where is the nail ten years later, when the tree is much taller? The nail is still one metre above the ground. The trunk below the tip does not stretch. All the new height was added at the top. You grow differently. Your whole body grows until you are an adult, and then stops. A plant keeps their meristems for life, so a tree that is 500 years old still has tips as young as a seedling's.
examples: Pinch the tip off a tulsi shoot and that shoot stops getting longer. Side buds lower down then wake and grow.
Grass keeps a meristem at the bottom of each leaf, so a lawn keeps growing after it is cut or grazed.
A coconut palm has one growing tip at the top. If that tip is destroyed, the palm cannot make another.
explanations.art: A tree drawn twice, small and then tall, with a nail in the trunk at the same height both times and glowing dots at every shoot tip.

explanations.concept: The cambium: how a trunk gets thicker
explanations.definition: The cambium is a thin sleeve of dividing cells between the wood and the bark. Each year it adds new xylem on its inner side and new phloem on its outer side. That is how a stem becomes a trunk.
explanations.description: The cambium is only a few cells thick. When one of its cells divides, one of the two new cells stays in the cambium. The other becomes a xylem cell on the inside, or a phloem cell on the outside. The cambium makes much more xylem than phloem. Xylem cells are hard, so they stay where they are, year after year. This is why a trunk is nearly all wood. As the wood grows, the cambium and the bark are pushed outward. Old phloem is soft, so it gets crushed, and the outer bark stretches and cracks. That is why the bark of an old neem or tamarind is deeply furrowed. So the living, working phloem of even a huge tree is a thin layer just under the bark. This is why girdling kills. If a ring of bark is removed all the way round, the phloem is cut. Water still rises in the wood, so the leaves stay green. But no sugar reaches the roots. When the roots have used up their stores, they die, and then the whole tree dies.
examples: A wire or nylon rope tied tightly round a young trunk and forgotten can slowly girdle the tree as the trunk thickens.
Rubber tappers in Kerala cut only part of the way round the trunk, in a sloping line. They never cut a full ring.
Gardeners make new plants by 'gootee', or air layering. They take a ring of bark off a branch. Food collects above the ring, and roots grow there.
explanations.art: A wedge of trunk showing, from inside out: heartwood, sapwood, a thin bright cambium line, inner bark and outer bark, with arrows from the cambium pointing both ways.

explanations.concept: Growth rings: how wood records the seasons
explanations.definition: A growth ring is the wood added in one growing season. Where a tree has one growing season each year, the tree adds one ring each year.
explanations.description: At the start of a growing season, a tree has plenty of water and is opening new leaves. The cambium then makes wide xylem cells with thin walls, to carry a lot of water. This pale wood is called early wood. Late in the season, growth slows, and the cambium makes narrow cells with thick walls. This darker wood is called late wood. Then growth stops for the cold season or the dry season. When it starts again, wide pale cells lie right next to last season's narrow dark ones. That sharp line is what you see as a ring. In a good year, with enough rain and warmth, the ring is wide. In a drought, the ring is narrow. So a trunk keeps a record of every year the tree has lived. But rings can mislead. In a place that is warm and wet all year, a tree may grow without stopping and show no clear rings. A dry spell in the middle of the rains can make an extra, false ring. In a very bad year a tree may add no ring at all on one side. So scientists never trust one tree. They compare many.
examples: Teak grows in forests with a long dry season, so teak makes one clear ring each year.
Deodar and pine in the Himalaya stop growing in winter, so they make one clear ring each year too.
Many trees of the wet evergreen forests of the Western Ghats and the Andaman Islands have faint rings, or none that can be counted.
explanations.art: A close view across three rings, each with wide pale cells on the inner side grading to small dark cells, and a sharp line where the next ring starts.

explanations.concept: Reading rings: a calendar kept by trees
explanations.definition: Dendrochronology is the science of using tree rings to find dates and to learn about past weather. It works by matching the pattern of wide and narrow rings between trees.
explanations.description: All the trees of one kind in one region live through the same wet and dry years. So they share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, like a barcode. A scientist can match the inner rings of a living tree with the outer rings of an old beam from a house, and then match that beam with an even older log. In this way the calendar is carried back far beyond the age of any living tree. This matching is called cross-dating. Scientists do not need to cut a tree down. They drill out a core of wood as thin as a pencil, and the tree seals the hole. Andrew Douglass, an American astronomer, built the method in the early 1900s. In 1929 he used it to date the wooden beams of ancient villages in the American Southwest. Florence Hawley was one of the first scientists trained in the method, and she carried it to new regions of North America in the 1930s. In India, scientists at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune and the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences in Lucknow read teak and deodar rings. From them they work out how strong the monsoon was in years long before anyone kept rain records.
examples: Teak rings from Kerala give a record of good and poor monsoon years that goes back about 500 years.
Deodar trees in the western Himalaya give ring records of several hundred years. The longest reach back to the 1300s.
A bristlecone pine in California, named Methuselah, has more than 4,800 rings. This pine is one of the oldest known living trees.
explanations.art: Three strips of wood with barcode-like ring patterns laid so their matching parts overlap, forming one long calendar.

explanations.concept: Sapwood, heartwood and bark: which parts are alive
explanations.definition: In a tree trunk, the outer wood, called sapwood, carries water. The inner wood, called heartwood, no longer does. The inner bark is living phloem, and the outer bark is dead cork.
explanations.description: Xylem pipes do not last for ever. After some years, air gets into them or they are plugged, and they stop carrying water. The tree then fills this old wood with resins and other substances that slow down rot. It turns darker and becomes heartwood. Every cell in heartwood is dead. Heartwood still helps to hold the tree up. In sapwood, the pipes are dead too, but thin sheets of living cells run through it and store food. So where is the living tree? The living tree is in the leaves, buds and root tips, in the cambium and inner bark, and in those living cells of the sapwood. In a great banyan or tamarind, that is a thin living layer wrapped round a core of dead wood. This explains why an old tree with a hollow trunk can stand green and healthy. Fungi have eaten the dead heartwood, but the living layer and the working sapwood are whole. Outer bark is made by a second cambium, the cork cambium. Cork cells fill with a waxy substance and die. They keep water in, and keep out insects, fungi and the heat of small fires.
examples: Old tamarind and banyan trees often have hollow trunks big enough for a child to stand in, and still bear leaves and fruit every year.
Sandalwood oil comes from the heartwood of the sandalwood tree, which grows in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Bottle corks and cork notice boards are the thick outer bark of the cork oak, peeled off without cutting into the living layer.
explanations.art: A hollow old tamarind tree in leaf, with a cut-away showing a thin green living layer round the hollow.

explanations.concept: Palms and bamboo: tall plants without rings
explanations.definition: Palms, bamboos and other monocots have no cambium sleeve. Their stems do not add a new layer of wood each year, so they have no growth rings.
explanations.description: A coconut palm's trunk is about as thick near the top as near the bottom. A young palm first spends some years growing wide at ground level. After that, the trunk grows up but hardly grows thicker. Its strength comes from hundreds of vascular bundles scattered through the trunk, each wrapped in hard fibres. Because there is no cambium, a palm cannot heal a deep cut in the trunk by growing new wood over it, as a mango tree can. A cut all the way round the surface does not usually kill a palm, though, because the phloem is spread all through the trunk and not gathered in a layer under the bark. Bamboo is a giant grass. A bamboo shoot comes out of the ground already at full width, and reaches full height in a few months. To guess the age of a coconut palm, people count the ring-shaped scars left by fallen leaves. A grown palm drops roughly a dozen leaves a year, so the count gives only a rough age.
examples: Coconut wood has no rings. The cut end of a palm trunk shows dark dots, which are the scattered bundles.
Bamboo scaffolding on building sites is strong for its weight because its hard fibres are packed near the outside of a hollow tube.
A banana 'trunk' is not a stem at all. It is a roll of leaf stalks wrapped tightly round each other.
explanations.art: A coconut palm trunk cut across showing dark dots scattered over the whole face, beside a mango log cut across showing rings.

explanations.concept: Pipes changed the world: how plants became tall
explanations.definition: The first land plants had no pipes and stayed a few centimetres tall. Plants with xylem and phloem appeared more than 420 million years ago. Wood appeared about 400 million years ago, and after that came forests.
explanations.description: A moss has no true xylem, so water has to soak from cell to cell. That is slow, so a moss stays small and lives in damp places. Fossils show that the first plants with pipes were thin green stalks with no leaves. Once plants could stiffen their pipes with lignin, they could stand taller and reach more light than their neighbours. Then some plants gained a cambium and began to make wood. By about 385 million years ago there were forests of real trees. This changed the planet. Roots broke rock into soil. Leaves took carbon dioxide out of the air. In the great swamps of that time, dead trunks piled up without rotting away, and were buried. Over millions of years, much of that buried wood became coal. Why did so much wood escape rotting? One idea is that few living things could yet digest lignin. Another is that the swamps were so waterlogged that wood rotted very slowly, whatever lived there. Scientists still argue about this. So the coal that still fuels many of India's power stations is mostly made from the stems, bark and wood of ancient plants. How tall can pipes carry a tree? The tallest tree known today is a coast redwood about 116 metres high. In 2004, George Koch and his team climbed the tallest redwoods and measured how hard it was for water to reach the top. They estimated a limit of about 122 to 130 metres. Nobody is sure the limit is right.
examples: Moss on a wet wall in the monsoon is only a few centimetres tall, because moss has no stiff pipes.
The coal mined at Jharia in Jharkhand and Singareni in Telangana formed from plants that lived more than 250 million years ago.
Fossil tree trunks about 20 million years old, turned to stone, can be seen at the National Fossil Wood Park at Tiruvakkarai in Tamil Nadu.
explanations.art: A timeline from a tiny moss to a thin leafless stalk to a tall ancient tree, with a lump of coal at the end.

explanations.concept: Do the pipes carry messages too?
explanations.description: Phloem carries more than food. Plants sense, remember and decide, and to do so their parts must tell each other things. Some of these messages are now known to travel in the phloem. A leaf senses how long the days and nights are. When they reach the right length, the leaf makes a small protein that travels in the phloem to the shoot tip, and the tip then starts making flowers. Scientists searched for this flowering signal for seventy years and found it in 2007. When a caterpillar bites one leaf, a signal races through the veins to far-off leaves in a minute or two, and those leaves begin making defence chemicals. In 2018, Masatsugu Toyota and his team filmed this as waves of light in a plant made to glow. Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata measured electric signals in plants a hundred years ago. In 1926 he wrote that the phloem carries them, and that this tissue works like a nerve. Scientists agree the signals are real. They disagree about what to call them.
examples: A spinach plant flowers when days grow long, because the leaves send a flowering signal to the tips through the phloem.
Touch one leaflet of a touch-me-not plant firmly and the folding spreads along the whole leaf, as a signal travels from part to part.
A bitten tomato leaf sets off defences in leaves the caterpillar has not reached yet.

perspectives.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, and today Stefano Mancuso, František Baluška and others
perspectives.explanation: Plants have a signalling system that does the work of a nervous system. They sense, pass on signals, remember and choose. The phloem is one of its main pathways.

perspectives.who: Lincoln Taiz and many other plant scientists
perspectives.explanation: The signals are real, but plants have no nerve cells and no brain. Words like 'nerve' and 'think' belong to animals and mislead when used for plants. The responses can be explained by chemistry.
Plants plainly process information in their own way. It is better to study how they do it than to argue about whether animal words fit.

explanations.art: A plant with a caterpillar on one leaf and a wave of light travelling along the veins to a far leaf.

agreed.text: Plants with veins have two transport tissues. Xylem carries water and minerals upward. Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks.
agreed.evidence: Dye in water shows up only in the xylem. Sugar marked with traceable carbon, fed to one leaf, is later found in the phloem and in roots, fruits and young leaves.

agreed.text: Working xylem pipes are dead, hollow cells. Working phloem pipes are living cells.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, xylem vessels are empty tubes with thick walls. Sieve tubes have a living lining, and they stop carrying sap when the cells are killed with heat, while the xylem beside them goes on carrying water.

agreed.text: A tree grows taller only at the tips and thicker only from the cambium.
agreed.evidence: Marks and nails on trunks stay at the same height for decades. Thin slices of a twig show the layer of dividing cells between wood and bark.

agreed.text: Removing a complete ring of bark kills most trees, because it cuts the phloem.
agreed.evidence: This has been repeated for 350 years. The bark swells above the ring, the leaves stay green at first, and the roots starve. Palms and other monocots are the exception, because their phloem is not in one layer.

agreed.text: Where the year has one growing season, trees add one ring a year, and ring width follows the weather.
agreed.evidence: Trees of known age, planted on a known date, have the right number of rings. Ring patterns match between trees of the same region, and match rain records where records exist.

agreed.text: Most of the wood in a tree trunk is dead, and the tree lives in a thin layer round that wood.
agreed.evidence: Stains that colour only living cells mark the inner bark, the cambium and scattered cells in the sapwood. They leave the heartwood blank. Hollow trees go on living.

challenging.claim: Sap goes round a plant the way blood goes round a body.
challenging.who: Several naturalists in the 1600s, after William Harvey showed that blood circulates
challenging.for: Liquid does move both up and down in a plant, and a little water does pass from the phloem back to the xylem.
challenging.against: A plant has no heart and no closed loop. Xylem sap and phloem sap are two different liquids in two separate sets of pipes. Most of the water that goes up leaves through the leaves and never comes back down. Stephen Hales argued this in 1727 from his measurements.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that a plant's sap circulates like blood.

challenging.claim: A tree trunk grows upward, so a mark on the trunk rises as the tree gets taller.
challenging.for: Trees do get taller every year, and low branches on old trees are often missing, which makes it look as if they moved up.
challenging.against: A trunk gets longer only at the tip. Nails, signs and carved names stay at the same height for the whole life of the tree. Low branches seem to rise because the old ones die and drop off.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief: that the whole trunk of a tree stretches upward.

challenging.claim: To find a tree's age, just count the rings. One ring is always one year.
challenging.for: It works well for teak, pine, deodar and other trees that have one clear growing season each year.
challenging.against: Some tropical trees make no countable rings. A dry spell in mid-season can add a false ring, and a very bad year can leave no ring. Scientists check by matching many trees.
challenging.context: This card is about the rule that one tree ring always equals one year.

challenging.claim: The heartwood is dead, so it is useless to the tree.
challenging.who: A common way of speaking about old trees
challenging.for: Heartwood carries no water and stores no food. Hollow trees can live for centuries without it.
challenging.against: Heartwood adds stiffness, and it is filled with substances that slow rot, which protects the trunk. Some engineers who study trees argue that a hollow trunk with a thick enough shell is nearly as strong as a solid one. Others find that hollow trees fail more often in storms.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the dead wood in the middle of a trunk is any use to a tree.

challenging.claim: The phloem is the nervous system of a plant.
challenging.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose in 1926, and some plant scientists today
challenging.for: Electric signals and chemical signals do travel through the phloem, quickly and over long distances. Plants use them to respond to wounds, touch and day length.
challenging.against: Plants have no nerve cells, no synapses and no brain. Many plant scientists say that calling phloem a nervous system stretches the word too far. They agree that the signals are real.
challenging.context: This card is about a bold claim: that a plant's food pipes also work like nerves.

big_questions.q: Most of a tree trunk is dead cells. So where does the living tree begin and end?
big_questions.hint: Think of a hollow tamarind tree that still bears fruit. Then think of your own hair and nails.

big_questions.q: A cambium cell makes wood on one side and bark on the other. How could one cell tell which side is which?
big_questions.hint: What might be different on the two sides: the squeeze, the signals from neighbours, the food arriving?

big_questions.q: A tree keeps a mark of every dry year in their rings. Is that a kind of memory?
big_questions.hint: What does a memory need? Does it need someone to read it? Do the tree's later rings depend on the earlier years?

big_questions.q: A xylem cell works only after dying. Can you think of anything else that does its job only after it has ended?
big_questions.hint: Think of a seed coat, a snail's shell, a spoken word, a fallen leaf feeding the soil.

big_questions.q: You stop growing when you are an adult. A tree keeps growing at the tips for life. Why might animals and plants differ in this?
big_questions.hint: An animal moves about to find food. A plant stays in one place and must grow toward what they need.

big_questions.q: If a rope slowly girdles a tree and nobody notices for years, how could the tree's own body tell the story afterwards?
big_questions.hint: Where would the trunk be fatter? What might the rings look like above and below the rope?

story.title: The Clothes Wire
story.note: A made-up story. Ammu, her family and the mango tree are imagined. The science is real. A wire left round a trunk can slowly cut off the bark as the tree thickens. A tree choked like this often flowers heavily before weakening, and the trunk swells above the wire. Rubber tappers in Kerala really do tap before sunrise, and they cut only part of the way round the trunk.
text: The mango tree behind Ammu's house had never flowered like this. In January every twig ended in a spray of tiny flowers. The tree stood over the yard like a yellow cloud, and the bees were loud from morning to dusk.
'A blessing,' said Thankamma from next door, looking over the fence. 'You will be giving away mangoes by the basket.'

By April there were no baskets. The mangoes had set in hundreds, small and hard as marbles. Then they dropped, a few every night. Ammu's little brother Unni collected them in a bucket and counted them. He got to two hundred and gave up.
In May the leaves began to go wrong. They were smaller than last year's, and pale, and the tree was thin enough to see the sky through.
'Water her,' said Thankamma. So Ammu and Unni carried buckets every evening. Nothing changed. 'Cow dung,' said Thankamma. Amma dug in two baskets of it. Nothing changed.
'She is drinking,' Amma said one evening, with her hand on a low branch. 'Look. Not one leaf is drooping. A thirsty tree droops.' She frowned at the tree for a while. 'I don't know what she wants.'
Amma knew trees. She tapped rubber on the Kuruvilla estate, three hundred trees before sunrise, and in the holidays Ammu went with her to carry the bucket.

They left at five, with lamps strapped to their heads. In the dark the rubber trees stood in rows, each with a sloping cut in the bark and a coconut shell hanging below it. Amma set her knife in yesterday's cut and drew it down along the slope. A ribbon of bark as thin as a fingernail curled away. White latex beaded on the fresh edge and began to run down toward the shell.
Ammu had watched this a thousand times. That morning she asked about it. 'Why do you stop halfway round? If you went all the way round, you would get twice as much.'
'For one season,' said Amma. She did not stop walking. 'Then you would have a dead tree.'
'Why?'

'The leaves make the tree's food. It comes down to the roots just here, under the bark.' She tapped the trunk with the back of her knife. 'Not in the wood. The wood carries water up. If you cut the bark the whole way round, the food has no road down. The top goes on looking fine. It has water, it has sun. And all that time the roots are starving in the ground. By the time the leaves tell you, it is too late.' She set her knife to the next tree. 'So we always leave her a road.'
They were home by nine. Amma slept. Ammu washed the school uniforms and carried them out to the line.

The clothes wire ran from a hook on the house to the mango tree. It went once round the trunk and was twisted to itself. It had been there since before Ammu was born. She threw Unni's shirt over the wire and reached to pull it straight. Her hand came to rest on the trunk.
Above the wire, the trunk bulged. It pushed out over the wire in a thick lip, like dough rising over the edge of a tin. Below the wire, the trunk was narrower, and the bark there looked dry.
She stood still with her hand on the lip. She thought of the food with no road down, and of the top that went on looking fine.

She walked round the tree with one finger on the wire. On the far side the wire was gone. The bark had closed over it, and only a seam showed where it lay inside. But near the twisted knot, the wire stood a little away from the trunk. Under the knot, a strip of bark as wide as her palm ran straight down, smooth and unbroken.
She woke Amma, which was not allowed.

Amma looked at the trunk for a long time without saying anything. Then she fetched the pliers. She cut the wire at the knot and pulled, and a hand's length came free. The rest would not move. She cut again where the wire went into the bark, and left the buried part where it was. 'If I dig that out, I do the wire's work for it,' she said.
She laid her hand flat on the smooth strip under the knot. 'This is all she has been living on. This one road.'
'Will she get better?' said Unni.
'I don't know,' said Amma. 'Ask her next year.'

The rains came in June. One wet afternoon Ammu went out under an umbrella and looked at the groove where the wire had been. Along its upper edge the bark had a new rim, rounded and tight. She scratched the rim gently with her thumbnail. Under the brown it was green.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the tree had plenty of water, because water travels in the wood, and the wire did not reach the wood. But a tree's food travels down in the phloem, just under the bark. The wire squeezed the bark shut nearly all the way round, so sugar piled up above it and the roots went hungry. That is why the tree flowered so heavily, why the trunk bulged above the wire, and why watering did not help.
ask: The leaves were not drooping, so the tree had enough water. What was the tree short of, and in which part?
Why did the trunk bulge above the wire and not below it?
Why did Amma leave the buried part of the wire inside the tree?
A rubber tapper cuts only part of the way round the trunk. What does that leave for the tree?
What would you look for on a tree near your home to check that nothing is choking the bark?

games.title: Xylem, Phloem, Both or Neither?
games.context: This is a card game about the two kinds of pipe in a plant. Each card gives a clue, and you say whether it fits xylem, phloem, both or neither.

printables.title: 20 clue cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Carries water and minerals up from the roots.
items.b: Xylem.

items.f: Carries sugar from a leaf to a growing fruit.
items.b: Phloem.

items.f: The working pipes are dead, empty cells.
items.b: Xylem. Each cell empties and dies before the pipe can carry water.

items.f: The working pipes are living cells.
items.b: Phloem. Sieve tube cells stay alive.

items.f: The flow goes one way only: up.
items.b: Xylem.

items.f: The flow can go up or down, toward a sink.
items.b: Phloem.

items.f: Turns blue when a stem stands in blue water.
items.b: Xylem. The dye travels with the water.

items.f: An aphid pushes her mouth tube into this to feed.
items.b: Phloem. She is after the sugar.

items.f: A teak door is made of this.
items.b: Xylem. Wood is old xylem.

items.f: In a tree, this lies in the inner bark.
items.b: Phloem.

items.f: The pipe walls are hardened with lignin.
items.b: Xylem. Lignin stops the pipe being squashed.

items.f: The end walls have holes, like a tea strainer.
items.b: Phloem. These walls are called sieve plates.

items.f: The cambium makes this.
items.b: Both. Xylem on the inner side, phloem on the outer side.

items.f: Runs through every vein of a leaf.
items.b: Both. Every vein holds xylem and phloem side by side.

items.f: Growth rings are made of this.
items.b: Xylem. Each ring is one season's new wood.

items.f: A complete ring cut in the bark of a mango tree cuts this.
items.b: Phloem. That is why girdling starves the roots.

items.f: Neera dripping from a cut coconut flower stalk comes from this.
items.b: Phloem. Neera is phloem sap.

items.f: The white latex of a rubber tree flows in this.
items.b: Neither. Latex has its own tubes in the inner bark, called latex vessels.

items.f: The waxy skin of a leaf is made of this.
items.b: Neither. The skin is epidermis, a different tissue.

items.f: Each pipe cell needs a companion cell alongside.
items.b: Phloem. The companion cell keeps the sieve tube cell alive.

items.p: Which tissue carries water up from the roots?

items.p: Which pipes are made of living cells?

items.p: True or false: food in the phloem can only travel downward.
