items.why: In a root the xylem is in the centre. In Pipe Maps the dye showed up in the carrot's pale core. A ring near the skin is the pattern of a stem.

items.p: Put these layers of a tree trunk in order, from the centre outward.
items.why: The oldest wood is in the centre. The cambium lies between the wood and the bark, with the living phloem just outside it.

items.p: True or false: a nail hammered into a tree trunk rises as the tree grows taller.
items.why: False. A tree grows taller only at the tips. The trunk below does not stretch, so the nail stays at the same height.

items.p: The thin layer between the wood and the bark that makes new wood is the ____.
items.why: The cambium is a sleeve of dividing cells. It adds xylem on the inside and phloem on the outside.

items.p: Draw a tree stump seen from above, with five rings. Then label the bark, one growth ring and the centre.
a: One growth ring: one band of wood
items.why: The centre is the oldest part, and the newest ring lies just under the bark.
items.art: A blank space for drawing a tree stump from above.

items.p: A teak stump has one very narrow ring among wide ones. What is the most likely cause?
opts: A bird nested in the tree
items.why: A narrow ring means the tree grew little that year. In teak the usual cause is a poor monsoon. Insects or a fire can do it too.

items.p: Why does a tree die if a ring of bark is removed all the way round the trunk?
items.a: The inner bark holds the phloem, which carries sugar from the leaves down to the roots. With the bark cut all the way round, no sugar reaches the roots. The roots use up their stores and die, and then the tree cannot take in water.
items.why: A strong answer says what the bark carries, where it was going, and why the leaves stay green at first: water still rises in the wood.

worksheets.title: Why the pipes are built this way (stretch)

items.p: Why must a xylem cell die before carrying water?
opts: An empty tube lets water through
items.why: A living cell is full of contents that would block the flow. Only an empty tube lets water pass easily. The death is switched on by the cell's own genes.

items.p: A sieve tube cell has no nucleus. How does it stay alive?
items.a: Each sieve tube cell has a companion cell alongside. The companion cell has a nucleus and makes what both cells need. The two are joined by tiny channels.
items.why: A strong answer names the companion cell and says why the sieve tube cell gave up the nucleus: to leave room for sap to flow.

items.p: True or false: when a stem stands in coloured water, the dye stains the phloem.
items.why: False. The dye travels with the water, so it stains the xylem. The phloem lies beside each coloured dot and stays unstained.

items.p: A part of a plant that takes sugar out of the phloem is called a ____.
items.why: Fruits, root tips, buds and stores are sinks. A part that gives sugar to the phloem is a source.

items.p: Sort these plants: are the pipe bundles in the stem in a ring, or scattered?
items.why: Grasses, palms and bamboo are monocots, with scattered bundles and straight leaf veins. Mango, hibiscus, tulsi and neem have a ring of bundles and net veins.

items.p: A stem bends in the wind. Where does strong tissue help it most?
items.why: When a rod bends, the outside is stretched and squeezed most. So strong tissue near the outside resists bending best. A root is pulled, not bent, so its strong tissue is in the centre.

items.p: Draw one vascular bundle from a stem. Label the xylem and the phloem, and show which side faces the skin.
items.a: A small oval with larger pipes on the inner side labelled xylem, and smaller cells on the outer side labelled phloem, with an arrow to the skin.
items.why: In a stem the phloem is on the outer side of each bundle and the xylem on the inner side.
items.art: A blank oval for one vascular bundle.

items.p: An old tamarind tree has a hollow trunk but is full of leaves and fruit. Two neighbours disagree.
items.a: A strong answer says the heartwood was dead already, and the living cambium, phloem and sapwood are whole, so the tree is alive and feeding. It also grants that a hollow trunk can be weaker in a storm, so the tree should be checked for safety.
items.why: Both have a point. Being alive and being safe near a house are two different questions.

views.says: The trunk is mostly gone. The tree is nearly dead and should be cut down.
The living part of a tree is the layer under the bark. This tree is healthy.

items.ask: Which neighbour do you agree with more? Use what you know about heartwood, sapwood and the cambium. Then say one thing the other neighbour has right.

items.p: Put the life of a xylem cell in order.
a: A new cell forms on the inner side of the cambium
The cell builds a thick wall with lignin
The cell breaks down everything inside and dies
items.why: The wall must be built while the cell is alive. The cell begins work as a pipe only after dying and emptying.
items: The cell builds a thick wall with lignin
A new cell forms on the inner side of the cambium
The cell breaks down everything inside and dies

items.p: A young leaf is a sink. Later the same leaf becomes a source. Explain what changes.
items.a: A young leaf is small and still growing, so it uses more sugar than it can make. Sugar comes in through the phloem. When the leaf is full size, it makes more sugar than it uses, and sends the extra out through the phloem.
items.why: A strong answer compares how much sugar the leaf makes with how much it uses.

items.p: Match each thing people use to the plant tissue it comes from.
items.why: People use every tissue of a plant. A strong answer can say what job each tissue did for the plant.
pairs: strong fibre cells in the stem's phloem

items.p: A tight nylon rope has girdled a tree for years. Where is the trunk fatter?
items.why: Sugar coming down in the phloem is held up above the rope, so the trunk grows more there. Below the rope the trunk is starved and stays thin.

items.p: Three of these are made of dead cells when they do their job. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A sieve tube is alive when it works. Xylem vessels, cork and heartwood are all dead cells that still do a job for the tree.

items.p: Why can nobody find the age of a coconut palm by counting rings?
items.a: A coconut palm has no cambium, so the trunk does not add a new layer of wood each year. The pipe bundles are scattered through the trunk, and there are no rings to count.
items.why: A strong answer names the missing cambium. It may add that leaf scars give a rough age.

items.p: The early wood in a growth ring looks pale. Why?
opts: Its cells are wide, with thin walls
Its cells are narrow, with thick walls
It has been dead for longer
items.why: Early in the season the tree makes wide pipes with thin walls, so there is more empty space and less wall. Late wood has narrow cells with thick walls, so it looks darker.

worksheets.title: Evidence and arguments about the pipes (challenge)

items.p: In early spring, sweet sap is tapped from the wood of sugar maples. Why is that surprising? Suggest an explanation.
items.a: It is surprising because wood is xylem, which usually carries water with very little sugar. In early spring the maple has no leaves yet. The tree turns starch stored in the wood into sugar and sends it up in the xylem sap to the buds.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the rule 'xylem carries water, phloem carries sugar' has exceptions, and reasons from the season: no leaves, so no working source in the crown.

items.p: Scientists agree that signals travel through the phloem. They disagree about what to call this.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: signals from a bitten leaf reach far leaves within minutes, and a touch-me-not folds leaflets far from the touch. It also grants that plants have no nerve cells or brain. It may say the plant does the same job in a different way.
items.why: Scientists agree on the measurements and disagree on the words. Plants sense, signal and respond through their whole body.

views.says: The phloem carries electric signals through the plant, as nerves do in an animal. Plants have a nervous system of their own kind.
The signals are real. But plants have no nerve cells and no brain, so the word 'nervous system' misleads.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give one piece of evidence. Then say what the other side has right.

items.p: An aphid's mouth tube is cut while she feeds, and sap keeps dripping from it. What does this show?
items.why: The aphid is gone, so nothing is sucking. The sap must be pushed out by pressure inside the sieve tube. This is strong evidence for pressure flow.

items.p: At a leaf, sugar is loaded into a sieve tube. Explain why water then moves into the sieve tube.
items.a: Water moves toward the place where it is held more tightly. Sugary sap holds water tightly. So water moves by osmosis from the xylem next door into the sieve tube. This raises the pressure there.
items.why: A strong answer uses osmosis, and links the extra water to higher pressure that pushes the sap along.

items.p: True or false: every tree in the world makes exactly one ring each year.
items.why: False. A tree makes one clear ring a year only where growth stops once a year. Some tropical trees make no clear rings, and odd weather can add a false ring or leave one out.

items.p: Why do scientists compare the rings of many trees before trusting a date?
opts: One tree can have false or missing rings
Old trees are hard to find
Every tree has a different pattern
items.why: A single tree may skip a ring in a very bad year or add a false one. A pattern shared by many trees is far more trustworthy. Trees of one region share their pattern, which is what makes matching possible.

items.p: A friend says dye soaks up a stem like ink into chalk. Give two observations that argue against this.
items.a: First, only small dots on the cut face are coloured, not the whole face. Second, when the stem is cut along its length, the colour runs in thin lines. Both fit pipes, and neither fits soaking.
items.why: A strong answer uses observations, not just the word 'xylem'. It may add that a leafy stem takes up colour faster than a bare one.

items.p: Wood is hard and stiff because its cell walls contain ____.
items.why: Lignin hardens and waterproofs the walls of xylem cells. It keeps the pipes open and holds the tree up.

items.p: Sort these cells. Is each one living or dead while at work?
items.why: Loading sugar and dividing need living cells. Carrying water, protecting and holding up are done by dead cells with strong walls.

items.p: Why could the first land plants, without xylem, not grow tall?
opts: They could not lift water or stand stiff
The air had no carbon dioxide
items.why: Without stiff pipes, water must soak slowly from cell to cell, and nothing hard holds the plant up. Xylem solved both problems at once.

items.p: Put the steps of dating an old beam by its rings in order.
a: Take a thin core from a living tree of the same region
Measure the width of every ring in the core and the beam
Find where the two patterns of wide and narrow rings match
Count from a ring of known year to the beam's last ring
items.why: The living tree gives known years, because the outermost ring is this year's. Matching the patterns carries those years across to the beam.
items: Find where the two patterns of wide and narrow rings match
Take a thin core from a living tree of the same region
Count from a ring of known year to the beam's last ring
Measure the width of every ring in the core and the beam

items.p: Much of the world's coal formed from ancient trees. Give one idea for why so much wood was buried without rotting.
items.a: One idea: lignin is very hard to digest, and when the first forests grew, few living things could break it down. Another idea: the swamps were waterlogged, and wood under water rots very slowly. Either way, fallen trunks piled up, were buried, and slowly became coal.
items.why: Either idea earns full marks. A strong answer links a property of wood or of the swamp to what happened to the whole Earth, and says scientists have not settled it.

items.p: Match each observation to what it shows.
items.why: Each of these is evidence. A strong answer can say what a different result would have meant.
pairs: Leaves stay green above a ring of removed bark
The bark swells above the ring
food travels down in the bark
Sap drips from a cut aphid mouth tube
A nail in a trunk stays at the same height
a tree grows taller only at the tips
One ring is much narrower than the rest
the tree grew little that year

items.p: Three of these are sinks. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A leaf in full sun makes more sugar than it uses, so it is a source. The other three take sugar from the phloem.

items.p: Draw a wedge of trunk from centre to bark. Label heartwood, sapwood, cambium, inner bark and outer bark. Shade the living parts.
a: Sapwood: outer wood, dead pipes with some living cells
items.why: The shaded living parts are the cambium and the inner bark, with scattered living cells in the sapwood. The heartwood and the outer bark are dead.
items.art: A blank wedge shape, like a slice of cake, for a piece of tree trunk.

experiments.title: Pipe Maps: where are the pipes in a root, a stem and a leaf stalk?
experiments.context: In this experiment a carrot, a leafy stem and a leaf stalk stand in coloured water overnight. Next day you cut each one across and map where the colour travelled.
experiments.question: Are the water pipes in the same place in a root, a stem and a leaf stalk? And how much of each part is pipes?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Draw three circles for the cut faces of a carrot, a stem and a leaf stalk. Mark with dots where you think the colour will show in each one. Will the pattern be the same in all three? Why do you think so? Write your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same coloured water, the same depth and the same number of hours for all three. Keep them side by side in the same place. Cut each one 3 centimetres above the level of the coloured water. Below that level the colour may have soaked in from the side. Only the plant part changes.
results_table: Where I guessed the pipes are
Where the coloured dots are (centre, ring or arc)
About how much of the cut face is coloured

materials.item: a fresh carrot, with the green tops still on if you can find one
the thickest leafy stems from a bunch of coriander or mint, or a chrysanthemum (sevanthi) stem from a flower seller
a leaf with a thick stalk: an outer leaf of a cauliflower or cabbage with its white rib, a palak leaf, or a celery stalk
food colour, dark blue or red: about 1 teaspoon of liquid for each glass, or 2 big pinches of powder
glasses or steel tumblers
a kitchen knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up only
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera to zoom in
a ruler, a pencil and plain paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Food colour stains clothes and stone floors, so work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Guess and draw. Stand the carrot, the stems and the leaf stalks in coloured water. Leave them overnight.
Cut each part across, map the coloured dots, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Draw each cut face as a circle as big as your palm, and mark every coloured dot where you see it. Fill in the table. Then write one sentence for what you found (your claim), one for what you saw (your evidence) and one for why you think the patterns differ (your reasoning).

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: How much of the face is coloured
rows: in the pale core at the centre
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A carrot, three leafy coriander stems and a cauliflower leaf standing in three glasses of dark blue water on a window sill.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a carrot, some leafy stems and a leaf stalk in coloured water. Leave them overnight.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand cutting across a stem on a chopping board, well above a blue stain line at the bottom of the stem.
setup.caption: 2. Next day, a grown-up cuts each one across, 3 centimetres above the water line.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at the cut end of a stem that shows a ring of blue dots, with a drawing of it on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Look at each cut face with a magnifying glass and draw where the coloured dots are.

flow.do: 1. Put the carrot, a stem and a leaf stalk on the table. 2. Ask your child to draw three circles, one for each cut face. 3. Ask them to mark where the colour will show, and to say why. 4. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: If we stand these in coloured water, where will the colour travel inside each one? Will all three look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw three circles. Mark where you think the colour will show. Say why.

good: The pipes are in the middle, like the lead in a pencil.
The whole inside soaks it up, like a sponge.
They are in strings, like the strings on the banana.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children expect the whole cut face to turn blue, or expect the same pattern in all three. Both are useful guesses to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pipe Maps. Here you guess where the water pipes are in a root, a stem and a leaf stalk.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into three glasses, about 3 centimetres deep. 2. Stir in food colour until the water is as dark as ink. 3. Cut 1 centimetre off the bottom of each stem and leaf stalk. 4. Cut the thin tip off the carrot, where the root is about as wide as a pencil. 5. Stand each kind in its own glass at once. 6. Put the glasses side by side in a bright, airy place, out of direct sun.
flow.say: A fresh cut opens the pipes. We keep all three in the same place, so that only the plant part is different.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the ends. Stand each one in the dark water. Put all three glasses together.
flow.parent: Leaves must stay on the stems, because water leaving the leaves pulls the colour up. A carrot with no green tops still works, but more slowly. Write down the time.
flow.context: This step of Pipe Maps sets up the test. A carrot, some stems and a leaf stalk go into coloured water.

flow.do: 1. After 1 hour, look at the leaves on the stems for the first signs of colour. 2. Then leave everything until tomorrow.
flow.say: Let's look at the leaf veins once before we leave it. Do you see any colour yet?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves after one hour. Is there colour in the veins? Now leave it all until tomorrow.
flow.wait: Leave it overnight, or for at least 4 hours
flow.context: This step of Pipe Maps is the wait. The coloured water needs hours to travel up inside each plant part.

flow.do: 1. Lift each one out and wipe the bottom. 2. Find the line where the coloured water reached on the outside. 3. Cut straight across, 3 centimetres above that line. 4. Look at each cut face with the magnifying glass. 5. Ask your child to draw each face as a big circle and mark every coloured dot.
flow.say: We cut above the water line, so we only see colour that travelled up inside. What do you notice on each cut face?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut each one across. Look closely at the cut face. Draw a big circle. Mark every coloured dot.

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: Only some small spots are coloured, not the whole face.
The dots are in different places in each one.
Most of the inside has no colour at all.

flow.parent: In the carrot, look inside the pale core. The colour may show as a patch, a star or a few dots at the edge of the core. If you see none, cut again 1 centimetre above the water line, because a carrot is slow. In a stem, the dots stand in a ring near the outside. In a leaf stalk, they lie in a curved row. If a coriander stem is too thin to see, take a photo and zoom in.
flow.context: This step of Pipe Maps is the cutting. Each part that stood in coloured water is cut across, so you can see where the colour travelled.

flow.do: 1. Count the coloured dots on each face and write the numbers in the table. 2. Write where the dots are: centre, ring or arc. 3. Ask how much of each face is coloured: less than a quarter, about half, or nearly all. 4. Cut one stem in half along its length and look inside.
flow.say: How many dots can you count? Where are they? And how much of the cut face has no colour at all?
flow.kid: Count the dots on each face. Write centre, ring or arc. How much of the face is coloured?

ask.q: When the stem is cut along its length, what do the dots turn out to be?
good: Long coloured lines running up the stem.
Each dot is the cut end of a long thin pipe.

flow.parent: The coloured part is usually well under a quarter of the face. The rest is packing tissue and skin. The dye shows only the xylem. A patch of phloem lies beside each dot, but the dye does not stain it.
flow.context: This step of Pipe Maps is the counting. You count the coloured dots on each cut face and say what pattern they make.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 2. Listen to all three before you say anything. 3. Then ask the question about pulling and bending. 4. Read the explanation card 'Where the pipes sit' together.
flow.say: Tell me what you found, what you saw that shows it, and why you think the three patterns differ.
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw that shows it. Say why you think the patterns differ.

ask.q: Wind tugs a root like a rope, and it bends a stem like a rod. Where would you put the strong pipes in each?
good: In the middle of the root, like the strands of a rope.
Near the outside of the stem, because the outside is stretched most when a rod bends.

flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. Claim: the pipes are in different places in each part. Evidence: the carrot had colour in the core, the stem had a ring of 9 dots, and the leaf stalk had an arc of 7. Reasoning: each part has to stand a different kind of force. Your child's own reasoning may be different, and that is fine if it uses the evidence.

check.q: In Pipe Maps, a stem that stood in dye showed a ring of dots. What is each dot?
options: A drop of dye that soaked in from the side
The cut end of a bundle of water pipes
A hole made by an insect
check.why: Each dot is the cut end of a vascular bundle, and the dye stains its xylem pipes. Choosing 'soaked in from the side' forgets that the cut was made above the water line. Cutting the stem along its length shows the dots are long lines.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pipe Maps. Here you say what the three dye patterns were, and think about why they differ.

experiments.title: Bark or Wood: which part of a twig carries the water?
experiments.context: In this experiment a fresh woody twig stands in coloured water for a day. Then you peel back the bark to see whether the colour travelled in the bark or in the wood.
experiments.question: A woody twig has bark on the outside, wood inside and a soft centre. Which of these carries water up to the leaves?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When a twig stands in coloured water, where will the colour travel: in the bark, in the wood, in the soft centre, or in all three? Draw your guess on a circle. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one twig, so the bark, the wood and the centre all get the same water for the same time. Compare them at the same height. Look only above the level of the coloured water.
results_table: Inner side of the bark: coloured or not?
Surface of the wood: coloured or not?

materials.item: a fresh woody twig with leaves, about as thick as a pencil and 25 centimetres long. A rose stem from a flower seller is easiest. A twig of hibiscus, curry leaf, guava or neem also works
food colour, dark blue or red
a glass or steel tumbler
a kitchen knife or a vegetable peeler, for a grown-up only
a ruler and a magnifying glass

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts and peels. Snip the thorns off a rose stem first. Food colour stains, so work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Guess and draw. Stand the twig in coloured water. Leave it for a day.
Peel windows in the bark at three heights, look at the bark and the wood, cut the twig across, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for each height. Draw the cut face of the twig and colour the part that the dye reached. Write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for a rose stem
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A leafy rose stem with thorns removed standing in a glass of dark blue water.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a fresh woody twig in coloured water for a day.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands peeling a small window of green bark off the twig with a knife, showing pale wood beneath with blue lines.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up peels a small window of bark, 5 centimetres above the water line.

setup.art: The twig cut across, with a blue ring in the wood, green bark outside it and a white centre.
setup.caption: 3. Cut the twig across and see which part is coloured.

flow.do: 1. Look at the cut end of the twig together. 2. Find the bark, the wood and the soft centre. 3. Ask your child to draw the cut face and colour in their guess. 4. Ask for the reason.
flow.say: This twig has bark, wood and a soft centre. Which part do you think carries water up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the cut end. Find the bark, the wood and the centre. Colour in your guess. Say why.

good: The bark, because it is wet and green underneath.
The centre, because it is soft like a sponge.
The wood, because trees are mostly wood.

flow.parent: Each of these guesses is reasonable. Do not say which is right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bark or Wood. Here you guess which part of a woody twig carries water.

flow.do: 1. Stir food colour into 3 centimetres of water until it is as dark as ink. 2. Hold the bottom of the twig under water in a bowl and cut off 2 centimetres. 3. Stand the twig in the coloured water at once. 4. Put it in a bright, airy place.
flow.say: We cut under water so that no air gets into the pipes. Now we leave the twig to drink for a day.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the end under water. Stand the twig in the dark water. Leave it for one day.
flow.parent: Keep the leaves on. If the leaves hang limp after an hour, cut the end again under water.
flow.context: This step of Bark or Wood sets up the test. A fresh twig goes into coloured water.

flow.do: 1. Lift the twig out and wipe it. 2. Measure 5 centimetres up from the water line. 3. There, peel off a window of bark about 2 centimetres long. 4. Look at the inner side of the peeled bark. 5. Look at the surface of the wood under it. 6. Write what you see in the table.
flow.say: Look at the inside of the bark, and then at the wood under it. Which one has the colour?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to peel a small window of bark. Look inside the bark. Look at the wood. Which is coloured?

good: The wood has coloured lines on it.
The bark is green or white inside, with no dye.
The bark peels off easily and the wood is slippery.

flow.parent: The bark of a fresh twig slips off easily. The wet, slippery surface is where the cambium was. Expect coloured streaks on the wood and clean bark.
flow.context: This step of Bark or Wood is the first look. A window of bark is peeled off a twig that stood in coloured water.

flow.do: 1. Peel another window at 10 centimetres and one at 15 centimetres. 2. Fill in the table for each. 3. Cut the twig straight across at 5 centimetres. 4. Look at the cut face with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: How high did the colour climb? And on the cut face, is the colour in the bark, the wood or the centre?
flow.kid: Look at two more windows higher up. Then ask a grown-up to cut across. Where is the colour?
flow.parent: On the cut face the colour is in the wood, often strongest in the outer part of the wood. The soft centre, called the pith, and the bark stay uncoloured.
flow.context: This step of Bark or Wood looks higher up the twig and at its cut face, to see where the colour travelled.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 2. Then ask what the bark might carry, if it does not carry the water. 3. Read the explanation card 'Two sets of pipes in every vein' together.
flow.say: What did you find, what did you see, and why do you think so? And if the bark carries no water, what could it be carrying?
flow.kid: Say what you found and what you saw. If bark carries no water, what could it carry?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. Claim: the wood carries the water. Evidence: at 5, 10 and 15 centimetres the wood was coloured and the bark was not. Reasoning: the wood is made of xylem pipes. The second question leads to phloem, the food pipes in the inner bark.

check.q: In Bark or Wood, the colour was in the wood and not in the bark. What does this show?
options: Bark is dead and does nothing
Water travels up in the wood
Wood soaks up dye from outside
check.why: The wood is xylem, and xylem carries water up. The inner bark is alive and carries sugar in the phloem, which this dye does not show. The windows were above the water line, so the wood was not stained from outside.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bark or Wood. Here you say which part of the twig carried the coloured water.

activities.title: String Hunt: find the strings in fruits and leaf stalks
activities.context: In this activity you pull the strings off a banana, an orange and a leaf stalk, and compare them. It is the first thing to do in this unit.

materials.item: a ripe banana
an orange or a mosambi
a thick leaf stalk: the white rib of a cauliflower or cabbage leaf, or a palak stalk
if you have one: a dry loofah scrubber (dried ridge gourd) or a piece of coconut husk

activities.record: Draw the banana with its strings. Add arrows to show which way you think something travelled along them, and write what you think it was.

setup.art: A peeled banana on a plate with three pale strings pulled away and laid beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Peel a banana and pull off the strings.

setup.art: A child's hands snapping a white cauliflower leaf rib and pulling the two halves apart, with thin strings stretching between them.
setup.caption: 2. Snap a leaf stalk gently and pull the halves apart slowly.

setup.art: A peeled orange with white threads on its surface, beside the banana strings.
setup.caption: 3. Find the white threads on a peeled orange and compare.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to peel the banana slowly. 2. Ask them to pull one string off, from the stalk end to the tip. 3. Ask what they notice and what the strings might be for.
flow.say: Look at these strings. Which way do they run? What do you think they are for? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Peel the banana slowly. Pull off one string. Which way does it run? What is it for?

ask.q: What do you think the strings are for?
good: To hold the peel on.
To carry something into the banana.
They are like veins.

flow.parent: Take every guess. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of String Hunt. Here you pull a string off a peeled banana and guess what it is for.

flow.do: 1. Bend the leaf stalk until it just snaps. 2. Pull the two halves apart very slowly. 3. Look for strings stretching between them. 4. Peel the orange and find the white threads on the fruit. 5. If you have a loofah or coconut husk, look at its fibres too.
flow.say: Pull slowly and watch the gap. What is still holding the two halves together?
flow.kid: Snap the leaf stalk gently. Pull the halves apart slowly. What stretches across the gap? Now peel the orange.
flow.parent: The strings in the leaf stalk are stronger than the soft tissue round them, so they break last.
flow.context: This step of String Hunt looks for strings in a leaf stalk and on a peeled orange.

flow.do: 1. Lay the strings side by side. 2. Ask what is the same about them. 3. Ask how you could test whether they carry water.
flow.say: What is the same about all these strings? If they are pipes, how could we test that?
flow.kid: Put the strings side by side. What is the same? How could you test what they carry?

ask.q: How could we test whether the strings carry water?
good: Put the stalk in coloured water and see if the strings change colour.
Cut one and see if water comes out.

flow.parent: Your child's test idea leads straight into Pipe Maps, which uses coloured water.

check.q: Banana strings, orange threads and leaf stalk strings all run the same way. Which way?
options: Round the fruit or stalk in rings
Lengthwise, from the stalk end outward
check.why: They all run lengthwise from where the part joins the plant. That fits pipes that carry water and food in from the plant. Rings would fit a wrapping, not a pipe.

flow.context: This is the last step of String Hunt. Here you compare strings from a banana, an orange and a leaf stalk.

activities.title: The Sweet Ring: taste the two halves of a carrot
activities.context: In this activity you taste the pale core and the orange outer ring of a carrot with your eyes shut. You find out whether one is sweeter.

materials.item: fresh carrots
a knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up only
two small plates marked A and B
a glass of drinking water
paper and a pencil for a tally

activities.record: Make a tally: how many times the core was called sweeter, how many times the outer ring, and how many times nobody could tell.

setup.art: A carrot slice seen from above with a pale yellow core and an orange outer ring, the two parts being cut apart.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts slices and separates the pale core from the orange ring.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut tasting a small piece of carrot, with two plates marked A and B and a glass of water.
setup.caption: 2. Taste A and B with your eyes shut, with a sip of water in between.

setup.art: A tally sheet with marks under 'core', 'outer ring' and 'can't tell'.
setup.caption: 3. Tally which piece tasted sweeter.

flow.do: 1. Cut six slices of carrot, each as thick as a finger. 2. Look at a slice together and find the pale core and the orange outer ring. 3. Ask which part your child expects to be sweeter, and why.
flow.say: A carrot slice has a pale core and an orange ring. Which do you think is sweeter? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at a carrot slice. Find the core and the outer ring. Which will be sweeter? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sweet Ring. Here you look at a slice of carrot and guess which part is sweeter.

flow.do: 1. Cut the core out of each slice. 2. Put the cores on plate A and the outer rings on plate B. 3. The taster shuts their eyes. 4. Hand them one piece from each plate, in an order they cannot guess. 5. They sip water in between and say which was sweeter. 6. Do this six times, with different tasters if you can.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Here is the first piece. Now a sip of water. Here is the second. Which was sweeter?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Taste one piece. Sip water. Taste the other. Which was sweeter?
flow.parent: Tasting with eyes shut keeps the test fair, because the taster cannot pick by colour. Many tasters find the outer ring sweeter. Carrots differ, so your result may not be clear. Write down what you really find.
flow.context: This step of the Sweet Ring is the blind tasting. You taste the core and the outer ring of a carrot without knowing which is which.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally. 2. Ask your child what they found. 3. Then tell them which tissue is which.
flow.say: What does our tally show? Now here is a clue. The core is the carrot's xylem. The orange ring grew on the phloem side.
flow.kid: Count your tally. Which part won? The core is xylem. The orange ring is on the phloem side.

ask.q: Phloem brings sugar down from the leaves. How might that explain your result?
good: The sugar arrives in the outer part, so more is stored there.
The core is for water, so it is less sweet.

flow.parent: The orange ring is phloem tissue, mostly storage cells that the phloem pipes feed. The core is xylem tissue. When scientists measure carrots, they usually find more sugar in the outer ring.

check.q: In a carrot, the cambium is the thin line between the core and the outer ring. What lies inside that line?
check.why: The cambium makes xylem on its inner side and phloem on its outer side, in a carrot as in a tree trunk. So the core is xylem. Choosing phloem mixes up the two sides.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Sweet Ring. Here you count which part of the carrot tasted sweeter and learn which tissue is which.

activities.title: Ring or Scatter? Two ways to arrange pipes in a stem
activities.context: In this activity you look at the cut stem of a grass or a lily relative, such as sugarcane or tuberose. You compare its pipes with the ring of dots you saw in Pipe Maps.

materials.item: one of these: a piece of sugarcane, a tuberose (rajnigandha or sampangi) stalk from a flower seller, or a fresh maize stalk
a leafy stem of coriander, mint or chrysanthemum, as in Pipe Maps
food colour and two glasses, if you use tuberose or maize
a knife, for a grown-up only, and a magnifying glass

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Sugarcane is hard, so cut it on a firm board.

schedule.what: Stand the tuberose or maize stalk and the leafy stem in coloured water overnight. Sugarcane needs no colour.
Cut both across, compare the patterns, and sort five plants by their leaf veins.

activities.record: Draw the two cut faces side by side. Label one 'ring' and one 'scatter'. Under each, write the names of two more plants you think belong with it.

setup.art: A tuberose stalk and a coriander stem standing in two glasses of blue water.
setup.caption: 1. Stand both stems in coloured water overnight.

setup.art: Two cut faces side by side: one with blue dots in a ring near the edge, one with blue dots scattered all over.
setup.caption: 2. Cut both across and compare the two patterns.

setup.art: A grass leaf with straight side-by-side veins beside a hibiscus leaf with a net of veins.
setup.caption: 3. Look at leaf veins: straight lines or a net?

flow.do: 1. Stand the tuberose or maize stalk in dark coloured water. 2. Stand the leafy stem in a second glass. 3. Ask your child to guess whether the two patterns will match, and why. 4. Leave both overnight. 5. If you have sugarcane, skip the colour, because its dots show without it.
flow.say: In Pipe Maps the stem had a ring of dots. Will this stem have a ring too? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand both stems in dark water. Will both show a ring of dots? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ring or Scatter. Here two different stems go into coloured water.

flow.do: 1. Cut each stem across, 3 centimetres above the water line. 2. Cut a thin slice off the end of the sugarcane, if you have one. 3. Look at the cut faces with the magnifying glass. 4. Ask your child to draw both.
flow.say: Look at both cut faces. Where are the dots in each one?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut both stems. Look closely. Where are the dots in each one?
flow.parent: Tuberose, maize and sugarcane show dots scattered over the whole face. Coriander, mint and chrysanthemum show a ring. If a tuberose stalk shows little colour, cut 1 centimetre above the water line.
flow.context: This step of Ring or Scatter is the cutting. You compare the dots on the cut faces of two kinds of stem.

flow.do: 1. Look at a leaf of grass, maize, banana or coconut. 2. Look at a leaf of hibiscus, mango or tulsi. 3. Ask how the veins differ. 4. Ask your child to sort five plants they know into 'ring' or 'scatter' by their leaf veins.
flow.say: Plants with scattered bundles mostly have straight veins lying side by side. Plants with a ring mostly have a net of veins. Which plants go where?
flow.kid: Look at a grass leaf and a hibiscus leaf. How do the veins differ? Sort five plants.

check.q: A coconut leaf has straight veins lying side by side. How are the pipe bundles arranged in a coconut trunk?
options: In one ring under the bark
check.why: Coconut is a monocot, like grass, maize and sugarcane. Monocots have bundles scattered through the stem. A single ring under the bark is the pattern of mango, neem and most other broad-leaved trees.

flow.context: This is the last step of Ring or Scatter. Here you link the pattern of pipes in a stem to the pattern of veins in a leaf.

activities.title: Read a Tree's Diary: twelve rings and an old beam
activities.context: In this activity you draw the rings of a made-up teak tree from a list of ring widths. You find the dry years, and then use the pattern to date an old wooden beam.

materials.item: plain paper, a sharp pencil and a ruler marked in millimetres
a strip of paper about 2 centimetres wide and 10 centimetres long

activities.record: Keep your drawn core strip and your beam strip. Write which years were dry, and the year in which the beam's tree made the last ring.

chart.title: A made-up teak tree: ring width and rain for 12 years (year 1 is at the centre)
chart.note: These numbers are made up for practice. Real teak rings follow the rain in a similar way, but less neatly.

setup.art: A pencil line on paper with a dot at the left end marked 'centre' and small cross marks along it at uneven gaps, each gap labelled with a year number.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line from the centre and mark off each ring width in millimetres.

setup.art: The marked line with three narrow gaps circled, beside a small table of rain.
setup.caption: 2. Circle the narrow rings and compare them with the rain table.

setup.art: A narrow paper strip with seven marks being slid along the longer drawn line until the marks match.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the beam strip along your core until the pattern matches.

flow.do: 1. Draw a straight line 6 centimetres long. 2. Mark a dot at the left end and label it 'centre'. 3. Read out the ring widths in order: 6, 5, 6, 2, 5, 4, 1, 2, 5, 6, 4, 5 millimetres. 4. Your child measures each width along the line from the last mark and makes a small cross mark. 5. Number the gaps 1 to 12.
flow.say: Scientists drill out a thin core of wood from the bark to the centre. Our line is that core. Each gap is one year of growth.
flow.kid: Draw a line. Mark off each ring width in millimetres. Number the gaps 1 to 12.
flow.parent: The twelve widths add up to 51 millimetres, so the line fits easily on a page. Check that the last mark is 51 millimetres from the centre.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read a Tree's Diary. Here you draw a core of a made-up teak tree from a list of ring widths.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to circle the three narrowest rings. 2. Ask what might have happened in those years, and why. 3. Only then show the rain column of the table. 4. Compare the narrow rings with the rain.
flow.say: Which three rings are narrowest? What do you think happened in those years? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Circle the three narrowest rings. What happened in those years? Say why. Then check the rain table.

ask.q: What could make a ring narrow, other than little rain?
good: Insects eating the leaves.
A taller neighbour taking the light.
A fire, or a broken branch.

flow.parent: The narrow rings are years 4, 7 and 8, and those are the three years with the least rain. Praise any other sensible cause too. Real scientists have to rule those out by comparing many trees.
flow.context: This step of Read a Tree's Diary finds the narrow rings of a made-up teak tree and compares them with a table of rain.

flow.do: 1. On the paper strip, draw a line and mark these widths in order: 6, 2, 5, 4, 1, 2, 5 millimetres. 2. Label the last gap 'outermost ring, next to the bark'. 3. Tell your child the strip is from an old roof beam from the same forest. 4. Ask them to slide the strip along the core until the pattern matches. 5. Ask which year the beam's last ring was made.
flow.say: This strip is from an old roof beam. Nobody knows when its tree was cut. Can the pattern tell us?
flow.kid: Mark the beam's rings on a strip. Slide the strip along your core. Where does the pattern match?

ask.q: In which year did the beam's tree make the last ring? How do you know?
good: Year 9. The beam's pattern 6, 2, 5, 4, 1, 2, 5 matches years 3 to 9 of the core.
The two very narrow rings close together gave it away.

flow.parent: The beam's seven rings match years 3 to 9. So the beam's tree was cut after the growing season of year 9. This matching is called cross-dating.
flow.context: This step of Read a Tree's Diary is a puzzle. You match the ring pattern of an old beam with the core of a tree whose years are known.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether this method would work on any tree. 2. Talk about a coconut palm and a tree from a forest that is wet all year. 3. Do the check.
flow.say: Would ring reading work on every tree? What does a tree need to do, to make one clear ring a year?
flow.kid: Would this work on every tree? What about a coconut palm? Say why.

check.q: Why does a teak tree make one clear ring each year?
options: Teak stops growing in the dry season
check.why: A ring shows where growth stopped and started again. Teak drops their leaves and rests in the dry season, once a year. A tree that never stops growing leaves no clear line. Hardness has nothing to do with it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Read a Tree's Diary. Here you think about which trees keep a diary in rings and which do not.

activities.title: Wood Hunt: find rings and grain at home
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at wooden things at home. You find the lines made by old growth rings, and you test which way wood splits.

materials.item: wooden things with a bare surface: a chopping board, a rolling pin, a door edge, a pencil, a wooden spoon
wooden ice cream sticks
a magnifying glass

activities.record: Draw the end of one wooden thing with its curved ring lines, and the side with its long grain lines. Write which way the ice cream stick split.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at the end of a wooden chopping board, where curved lines show.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the cut end of a wooden board for curved lines.

setup.art: The side of the same board showing long, nearly straight lines.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the side for long lines. This is the grain.

setup.art: Two ice cream sticks, one split neatly along its length and one snapped across with a jagged edge.
setup.caption: 3. Split one ice cream stick along its length and snap one across.

flow.do: 1. Find a wooden thing with a bare cut end, such as a chopping board or the top edge of a door. 2. Look at the end with the magnifying glass. 3. Then look at a long side. 4. Ask how the lines differ.
flow.say: Look at the end of this board, and then at its side. How are the lines different? What could have made them?
flow.kid: Look at the end of the board. Now look at the side. How are the lines different?

ask.q: What made the curved lines on the end?
good: They are parts of growth rings.
Each one is the edge of a year's wood.

flow.parent: On the end you see curved lines, which are parts of growth rings. On the side the same rings show as long lines, called the grain. Some woods, such as mango wood and rubber wood, show rings only faintly. Pine and teak show them clearly.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wood Hunt. Here you compare the lines on the end and on the side of a piece of wood.

flow.do: 1. Hold an ice cream stick by its two long edges and bend it until it splits along its length. 2. Hold a second stick by its two ends and bend it until it snaps across. 3. Compare the two breaks.
flow.say: Which break was easier? Which edge is straight, and which is jagged? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Split one stick along its length. Snap another across. Which was easier? Which edge is jagged?
flow.parent: The stick splits along its length with a clean line and snaps across with splinters. The wood cells are long pipes and fibres lying lengthwise. Splitting pulls them apart from each other. Snapping has to break each one.
flow.context: This step of Wood Hunt tests which way wood splits, using two ice cream sticks.

flow.do: 1. Ask the nail question. 2. Let your child answer and give a reason. 3. Then read the explanation card 'Meristems' together.
flow.say: Someone hammers a nail into a tree, one metre up. In ten years the tree is twice as tall. How high is the nail? Why?
flow.kid: A nail is one metre up a tree. The tree doubles in height. How high is the nail now?

check.q: A nail is hammered into a trunk 1 metre above the ground. Ten years later the tree is twice as tall. How high is the nail?
check.why: A tree grows taller only at the tips of the shoots. The trunk below does not stretch, so the nail stays at 1 metre. Choosing 2 metres means thinking the whole trunk stretches, as a child's leg does.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wood Hunt. Here you think about where a tree grows, using a puzzle about a nail.

activities.safety: A snapped ice cream stick has sharp splinters. Put the pieces in the bin straight away.

activities.title: Build the Two Pipes: a paper model of xylem and phloem
activities.context: In this activity you build one xylem pipe and one phloem pipe from rolled paper. The model shows why one is empty and the other has strainer walls.

materials.item: sheets of used notebook paper
sticky tape and scissors
a sharp pencil for making holes
thread or wool, about 1 metre
uncooked rice or rava
a plate

activities.record: Draw your two models. Label: hard wall, open end, sieve plate, companion cell. Write one way the model is like the real pipe and one way it is not.

setup.art: Three short paper tubes taped end to end into one long open tube, with thread wound round it in a spiral.
setup.caption: 1. Xylem: tape three open tubes end to end and wind thread round them.

setup.art: Three short paper tubes joined end to end with a paper disc full of pencil holes between each pair, and a thin paper tube taped alongside.
setup.caption: 2. Phloem: join three tubes with a holed paper disc between each pair. Tape a thin tube beside them.

setup.art: A child pouring rice into the top of each tube over a plate.
setup.caption: 3. Pour rice through each pipe and compare.

flow.do: 1. Roll three sheets into tubes about as wide as two fingers, and tape them. 2. Tape the three tubes end to end, so they make one long open pipe. 3. Wind thread round the pipe in a spiral and tape the ends. 4. Tell your child each tube stands for one dead, empty cell.
flow.say: Each tube is one xylem cell. The end walls are gone. The thread is the hard lignin that stops the pipe being squashed.
flow.kid: Roll three paper tubes. Tape them end to end. Wind thread round them. This is a xylem pipe.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build the Two Pipes. Here you make a paper model of a xylem pipe.

flow.do: 1. Roll three more tubes. 2. Cut two paper circles a little wider than a tube, and push about ten holes through each with the pencil. 3. Tape one holed circle between each pair of tubes, to join them. 4. Roll a thin tube and tape it along the side. 5. Tell your child the holed circles are sieve plates and the thin tube is a companion cell.
flow.say: Each tube is one living phloem cell. The holed walls are sieve plates. The thin tube beside them is a companion cell, which keeps the cell alive.
flow.kid: Roll three more tubes. Join them with holed paper circles. Tape a thin tube beside them. This is phloem.
flow.parent: Make the holes a little wider than a grain of rice. A grown-up may need to help with the holed circles.
flow.context: This step of Build the Two Pipes makes a paper model of a phloem pipe, with sieve plates and a companion cell.

flow.do: 1. Hold each pipe upright over the plate. 2. Ask your child to guess which pipe the rice will pass through faster, and why. 3. Pour a spoonful of rice into the top of each. 4. Talk about where the model is like the real pipe and where it is not.
flow.say: Which pipe will the rice pass through faster? Why do you think so? Now pour, and watch.
flow.kid: Guess which pipe lets rice through faster. Say why. Pour rice into each. What happened?

ask.q: How is the model not like the real thing?
good: Real pipes are thinner than a hair.
Real sap is pulled or pushed, it does not fall.
Real phloem can carry sap upward too.

flow.parent: The rice runs straight through the open pipe and slowly through the sieve plates. Every model is wrong somewhere, and finding where is part of the science.

check.q: Why does a xylem pipe need walls hardened with lignin?
options: To stop the pull on the water squashing the pipe
check.why: Water in the xylem is pulled from above. That pull would flatten a soft pipe, as a paper straw flattens when you suck hard. Lignin keeps the pipe open and also helps hold the plant up.

flow.context: This is the last step of Build the Two Pipes. Here you pour rice through paper models of xylem and phloem and compare them.

projects.title: Gootee: grow roots on a branch in the air (if you have a woody pot plant or a garden)
projects.context: In this six-week project a grown-up removes a ring of bark from one branch of a woody plant and wraps the place in damp coco peat. You watch where roots grow. Gardeners in India call this gootee, or air layering.

materials.item: a healthy woody plant with a branch as thick as a pencil: hibiscus, croton, rubber plant, guava, pomegranate or bougainvillea
a sharp clean knife, for a grown-up only
damp coco peat, or damp soil mixed with compost
a piece of clear plastic sheet about 20 centimetres square, and string
a notebook for a weekly diary

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting, and cuts away from the hand that holds the branch.

schedule.what: Guess what will happen. A grown-up removes a ring of bark. Wrap the place in damp coco peat and plastic.
Look through the plastic. Are the leaves above the ring still fresh? Draw what you see.
Look for a swelling at the upper edge of the ring. Add water with a spoon if the coco peat looks dry.
Look for white root tips. Note whether they come from the upper edge or the lower edge.
Look again and draw the roots.
Look again. Count the roots you can see.
If there are many roots, a grown-up cuts the branch off below them and you plant the branch in a pot. Write what you found.

projects.record: Keep a diary with one drawing each week. Each time, note three things: are the leaves above the ring fresh, is there a swelling, and where are the roots. At the end write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands removing a ring of bark 2 centimetres wide from a hibiscus branch, leaving pale wood showing.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up removes a ring of bark 2 centimetres wide.

setup.art: A ball of damp coco peat wrapped round the ringed part of the branch inside clear plastic, tied at both ends like a toffee.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap the place in damp coco peat and clear plastic, and tie both ends.

setup.art: The same wrapped branch weeks later, with white roots showing through the plastic at the upper edge of the ring only.
setup.caption: 3. Each week, look for a swelling and for roots.

flow.do: 1. Choose a healthy branch as thick as a pencil. 2. About 30 centimetres below its tip, cut two rings through the bark, 2 centimetres apart. 3. Peel off the ring of bark between them. 4. Scrape the wet, slippery layer off the bare wood. 5. Ask your child to guess what will happen above and below the ring, and why. 6. Wrap damp coco peat round the place, cover it with plastic and tie both ends.
flow.say: We have taken away the bark but left the wood. Will the leaves above stay alive? Where might something new grow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up takes a ring of bark off. Will the leaves above live? Where will something new grow? Say why.
flow.parent: Cut only through the bark, not into the wood. Scraping off the slippery layer removes the cambium, so that the bark does not simply grow back. The warm, wet months from June to September are best. Squeeze the coco peat first, so that it is damp but not dripping.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Gootee project. A ring of bark comes off a branch, and you guess what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Once a week, look through the plastic without opening it. 2. Check the leaves above the ring. 3. Look at the upper and lower edges of the ring. 4. Add a spoonful of water at the top if the coco peat looks pale and dry. 5. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Are the leaves above the ring still fresh? What does that tell us about where the water travels? What is happening at the two edges?
flow.kid: Each week, look through the plastic. Are the leaves fresh? Is there a swelling? Are there roots? Draw them.

ask.q: The leaves above the ring are still fresh. So where does the water travel?
good: In the wood, because the bark is gone and water still gets past.
In the xylem.

ask.q: Why is the swelling at the upper edge and not the lower edge?
good: Food coming down from the leaves is stuck there.
The phloem is cut, so sugar piles up above the ring.

flow.parent: This step is five short checks of 5 minutes each, on days 8, 15, 22, 29 and 36. Expect fresh leaves, then a pale swelling at the upper edge after 2 or 3 weeks, then roots from that swelling. Roots take 4 to 8 weeks, and longer in cool weather. If the branch dries up above the ring, the cut went too deep into the wood. That is a result too: write it down and try another branch.
flow.context: These are the weekly checks of the Gootee project. You look at a branch with a ring of bark removed, to see where it swells and grows roots.

flow.do: 1. When many roots show through the plastic, cut the branch off just below them. 2. Unwrap the plastic gently. 3. Plant the rooted branch in a pot and keep the pot in shade for a week. 4. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
flow.say: What did you find, and what did you see? Why did roots grow above the ring and not below it?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts below the roots. Plant your new plant. Say what you found and why.
flow.parent: If there are no roots yet, wrap the branch again and wait two more weeks. A good answer: water went up through the wood, so the leaves lived. Food came down in the bark and stopped at the ring, so the roots grew there.

check.q: In gootee, a ring of bark is removed from a branch. Why do roots grow at the upper edge of the ring?
options: Sugar coming down the phloem collects there
The upper edge gets more light
check.why: The phloem in the bark is cut, so sugar from the leaves cannot pass and collects above the ring. That food feeds new roots. Water is not blocked, because it travels in the wood.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Gootee project. A branch that grew roots above a ring of removed bark is cut off and planted.

challenges.title: Tap Without Killing: design a rubber tapper's cut
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. A rubber tapper must cut the bark to collect latex, but the tree's food also travels in the bark. You design a cut that collects latex and still lets food reach the roots.
challenges.problem: Wrap a sheet of paper round a bottle to make a trunk. Draw 24 lines from top to bottom. Each line is a strand of bark that carries food down and latex. Design one cut that crosses as many lines as you can, while at least 12 lines stay whole from top to bottom.
constraints: At least 12 of the 24 lines must stay uncut from top to bottom, so food can still reach the roots.
The cut must slope downhill all the way, so the latex runs along it to one cup.
A line that is cut even once counts as cut.
materials: a bottle or a rolling pin to wrap the paper round
a pencil and a red pen
general: Cut a sloping line half the way round the trunk. This is what rubber tappers in Kerala do.
Cut a V shape on one side, with the cup at the point of the V.
Cut a short sloping line a quarter of the way round, and accept less latex.
creative: Plan for several years: tap one half of the trunk while the bark on the other half grows back.
Shave off only a very thin strip from the same cut each day, as real tappers do, so that little bark is used up.
Try two short cuts at different heights, and check whether more than 12 lines are now cut.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own cut. Draw it in red on your paper trunk. Unwrap the paper and count the cut lines and the whole lines. Could your tree live with this cut for twenty years?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with 24 vertical pencil lines being wrapped round a bottle and taped.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 24 lines on paper and wrap it round a bottle.

setup.art: The paper trunk with a red sloping cut drawn half the way round and a small cup drawn at its lower end.

check.q: Why does a rubber tapper never cut a complete ring round the trunk?

Latex only flows on one side
check.why: Food from the leaves travels down in the phloem of the inner bark. A complete ring cuts every strand, so no sugar reaches the roots. Half the way round leaves half the phloem whole.

challenges.title: Build a Working Stem
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A real stem holds a plant up, carries water and keeps that water from drying out. You build a model stem from paper that does all three.
challenges.problem: Build a stem at least 12 centimetres tall that stands in a glass of coloured water without being held. It must hold a 5 rupee coin at the top. It must also carry coloured water up to a paper flower at the top within 30 minutes.
constraints: Use only paper, tissue or kitchen roll, drinking straws, thread and tape.
The flower must not touch the water or the glass.
Nobody may hold the stem or pour water on the flower.
materials: a glass with 3 centimetres of coloured water
general: Roll a strip of kitchen roll into a wick, and tape it to a rolled paper tube for strength.
Thread a wick of tissue through a straw, so the straw holds it up.
Use several thin wicks side by side, like a bundle of pipes.
creative: Wrap the wick in a skin of plain paper or tape, to slow the drying. Leave both ends open.
Put the stiff parts near the outside and the wick inside, like a real stem.
Make a taller stem of 20 centimetres, and time how much longer the colour takes.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own stem. Draw it and label the transport part, the support part and the skin. Build it and test it. How tall is it, and how long did the colour take to reach the flower?

It holds the plant up.

check.q: In a real young stem, which tissue both carries water and helps hold the stem up?
check.why: Xylem pipes have hard walls full of lignin. They carry water, and their stiffness helps hold the stem up. Phloem is soft, and the epidermis is a thin skin.

quiz.p: Which of these is a tissue?
quiz.why: The skin of a leaf is many cells of one kind doing one job, which makes it a tissue. One cell is too little, and a whole tree is many tissues and organs together.

quiz.p: A stem stands in red water overnight. Which part of each bundle turns red?
quiz.why: The dye travels with the water, and water travels in the xylem. The phloem beside it carries sugar and stays unstained.

quiz.p: Which sentence about phloem is true?
opts: Its pipes are dead and hollow
It carries sugar to wherever it is needed
quiz.why: Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks, up or down. Its pipes are living cells. 'Only downward' is the old idea that tracing experiments showed to be wrong.

quiz.p: The cut face of a stem shows bundles scattered all over it. Which plant is this most likely to be?
quiz.why: Maize is a grass, and grasses are monocots with scattered bundles. Mango, tulsi and hibiscus have their bundles in a ring.

quiz.p: Why are a root's strongest pipes gathered in its centre?
opts: A root is pulled, like a rope
The centre is the warmest part
quiz.why: Wind on the plant tugs the roots like ropes. A rope is strongest with its strong strands together in the middle. A stem is bent, so its strong tissue sits near the outside.

quiz.p: A bare teak tree starts growing new leaves. Where does the food to build them come from?
opts: From stores in the trunk and roots
quiz.why: With no leaves, nothing is making sugar. The stores in the trunk and roots become sources, and the phloem carries their food up to the buds.

quiz.p: A wire has been tight round a trunk for years. The leaves are green, but the tree is weakening. Why?
opts: The leaves get too much sun
quiz.why: The wire chokes the phloem in the inner bark, so sugar cannot get down to the roots. Water still rises in the wood, which is why the leaves stay green.

quiz.p: Where is the cambium in a tree trunk?
opts: Between the wood and the bark
quiz.why: The cambium is a thin sleeve between wood and bark. It adds xylem inward and phloem outward, which makes the trunk thicker.

quiz.p: A stump from a forest with one dry season a year has 40 clear rings. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.why: Where growth stops once a year, a tree adds one ring a year. So 40 rings mean about 40 years. Rings say nothing about height.

quiz.p: Why can ring counting fail for a tree in a forest that is warm and wet all year?
opts: Growth never stops, so no clear lines form
The wood is too hard to cut
The rings are too wide to see
quiz.why: A ring line forms where growth stops and starts again. A tree that grows all year may leave no clear line to count.

quiz.p: In a dye test, why do we cut the stem above the level of the coloured water?
opts: To see only colour that travelled up inside
quiz.why: Below the water line, colour may have soaked in from the side. Above it, any colour must have been carried up inside the stem. This keeps the evidence clean.

quiz.p: Which part of a big mango tree's trunk is made of living cells?
quiz.why: The cambium and the phloem of the inner bark are alive. Heartwood, outer bark and the water pipes themselves are dead cells that still do a job.

applications: Timber: every wooden door, bed and boat is xylem. Carpenters cut along the grain because the long cells lie that way.
Paper is made by breaking wood into its separate xylem cells and pressing them into a sheet.
Natural rubber comes from latex tubes in the inner bark of rubber trees. Most of India's rubber is tapped in Kerala.
Neera, toddy and palm jaggery come from phloem sap. Kamala Sohonie, the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, studied neera and found it a nourishing drink.
Grafting joins a branch of one mango variety to the roots of another. It works only if the two cambium layers touch and grow together.
Gardeners use gootee, or air layering, to make new guava, litchi and pomegranate plants from branches.
Tree rings tell scientists how strong the monsoon was in years before anyone measured rain. This helps them judge how unusual today's droughts and floods are.
Engineers have built water filters from short pieces of pine sapwood. The tiny holes between xylem cells hold back bacteria. Trials have been run with families in India.

open_questions.q: How does each new cell beside the cambium come to be wood or phloem?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found some of the signals that pass between the cells. But nobody can yet predict, cell by cell, what the cambium will make or how much.

open_questions.q: How do sieve tube cells stay alive for years with no nucleus?
open_questions.why_open: In palms, the same sieve tubes seem to work for many decades. The companion cells must supply them, but how they keep them going for so long is not known.

open_questions.q: Is pressure flow the whole story of how phloem sap moves in the tallest trees?
open_questions.why_open: Sieve tubes seal themselves when touched, so pressures inside them have been measured in only a few plants.

open_questions.q: How do plants use the signals that travel through their veins?
open_questions.why_open: Electric and chemical signals have been recorded moving through the phloem. What a distant leaf does with each kind of signal is only beginning to be worked out.

open_questions.q: Why do some tropical trees make yearly rings while their neighbours in the same forest do not?
open_questions.why_open: It seems to depend on how each kind of tree responds to dry spells, floods and leaf fall. For most tropical trees, nobody has checked.

open_questions.q: Is there a greatest height that a tree's pipes allow?
open_questions.why_open: One estimate is about 122 to 130 metres. It rests on measurements from a few redwoods, and other scientists think the limit is set by something else.

open_questions.q: Why was so much wood buried without rotting in the age of the coal swamps?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists point to lignin, which few living things could digest then. Others point to waterlogged ground and sinking land. The evidence does not yet settle it.

maths.problem: In Pipe Maps, you draw the cut face of a stem on squared paper. The face covers 80 small squares, and the coloured dots cover 8. What fraction of the face is coloured? What fraction is not?
maths.answer: One tenth is coloured. Nine tenths is not.
maths.explain: 8 out of 80 is 8/80. Divide top and bottom by 8 to get 1/10. The rest is 1 - 1/10 = 9/10. So nine tenths of the stem is other tissue: packing, skin and phloem.
maths.context: This is about Pipe Maps, where a stem stands in coloured water and you map the coloured dots on its cut face.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how much of a stem is water pipes more exactly than 'a little'.

maths.problem: A teak log is 30 centimetres across. Its rings are 3 millimetres wide on average. About how old was the tree?
maths.explain: Rings are counted from the centre to the bark, so use the radius, not the full width. The radius is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 centimetres, which is 150 millimetres. 150 ÷ 3 = 50 rings. Using the full 30 centimetres would count every ring twice and give 100.
maths.context: This is about Read a Tree's Diary, where you draw the rings of a teak tree from the centre outward.
maths.why_maths: Division turns a width you can measure into an age you cannot see.

maths.problem: In Read a Tree's Diary, the 12 ring widths are 6, 5, 6, 2, 5, 4, 1, 2, 5, 6, 4 and 5 millimetres. What is the mean ring width?
maths.explain: Add the widths: 6 + 5 + 6 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 5 = 51. Divide by the number of rings: 51 ÷ 12 = 4.25. So the mean is 4.25 millimetres.
maths.context: This is about Read a Tree's Diary, where you draw a made-up teak tree's rings from a list of widths.
maths.why_maths: The mean tells you what a normal year looks like, so that a narrow ring stands out as unusual.

maths.problem: In the made-up teak table, 1,000 mm of rain gave a 1 mm ring, 1,300 mm gave 2 mm, 1,900 mm gave 4 mm and 2,200 mm gave 5 mm. Predict the ring for a year with 1,600 mm of rain.
maths.explain: Look for the pattern. From 1,000 to 1,300 is 300 mm more rain, and the ring is 1 mm wider. From 1,900 to 2,200 is 300 more, and again 1 mm wider. So each extra 300 mm adds about 1 mm. 1,600 is 300 more than 1,300, so the ring is about 2 + 1 = 3 mm. A real tree would not follow the pattern this neatly.
maths.context: This is about Read a Tree's Diary, where a table shows the rain and the ring width for each year of a made-up teak tree.
maths.why_maths: Finding the pattern lets you run it backwards, as scientists do when they work out past rain from old rings.

maths.problem: A tree adds a ring 4 millimetres wide every year. How much wider is the trunk, measured straight across, after 10 years?
maths.explain: A ring goes all the way round, so it adds 4 mm on one side of the trunk and 4 mm on the opposite side. That is 8 mm wider each year. In 10 years: 8 × 10 = 80 mm, which is 8 centimetres. Answering 4 centimetres counts only one side.
maths.context: This is about Wood Hunt, where you look at growth rings on the cut end of a wooden board.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how thin yearly rings add up to a thick trunk.

maths.problem: Suppose phloem sap moves 1 metre in an hour and xylem sap moves 6 metres in an hour. In a coconut palm 18 metres tall, how long does each take to travel the whole height?
maths.answer: Phloem sap takes 18 hours. Xylem sap takes 3 hours.
maths.explain: Time is distance divided by speed. Phloem: 18 ÷ 1 = 18 hours. Xylem: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 hours. So sugar made at midday reaches the roots only the next morning. These speeds are example numbers. Real speeds change with the plant and the weather.
maths.context: This is about Feed the Plant, the card game where you deliver sugar from the leaf to the tip, the fruit and the root.
maths.why_maths: Working out the travel time shows that a delivery inside a tall plant takes hours, not seconds.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out which way food travels inside a plant? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: About 350 years ago, the Italian doctor Marcello Malpighi cut a ring of bark off a branch. The bark swelled above the cut. He reasoned that food made in the leaves travels down in the bark. For the next 250 years, most books said that food sap only sinks, from the leaves to the roots. In 1837 the German forester Theodor Hartig found the food pipes themselves, the sieve tubes. But nobody could collect clean sap from one tube, because a tube seals itself when cut. Then scientists noticed that aphids already tap single tubes. In 1953, John Kennedy and Thomas Mittler in England cut through an aphid's mouth tube while she was feeding. Sap went on dripping from the cut tube for hours. So the sap was under pressure, and it was full of sugar. In the same years, other scientists gave single leaves carbon dioxide made with a kind of carbon that can be traced. The marked sugar turned up in the roots below. It also turned up in young leaves and fruits above. So food does not only sink. Food goes to wherever the plant is using or storing it.
how_we_found_out.who: Marcello Malpighi, an Italian doctor. Theodor Hartig, a German forester. John Kennedy and Thomas Mittler, insect scientists working in England.
how_we_found_out.when: The 1670s (Malpighi's ring of bark), 1837 (Hartig's sieve tubes), 1953 (the aphid's mouth tube), and the 1940s and 1950s (traceable carbon).
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That food sap travels only downward, from the leaves to the roots. Traceable carbon showed sugar from one leaf moving up to fruits and young leaves as well as down to roots.
how_we_found_out.art: A tiny aphid on a stem with her mouth tube in the bark, and beside it the cut tube alone with a golden drop of sap forming at its end.

roots.context: We have learned that a plant has dead pipes for water and living pipes for food, and that a tree trunk is mostly dead wood inside a thin living layer. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Pipe Maps test, dye climbed through xylem pipes. Each pipe is a column of cells that built hard walls, then died and emptied. Water can pass only because those cells are dead. So a living tree depends on dead cells, and most of a trunk is made of them. In a tree, dying at the right time is one of the jobs a cell can have.
deep_truth.habit: We sort everything into 'alive' or 'dead', and we think a living body must be alive all the way through. We also think a cell that dies has failed. A tree shows that neither is true. A xylem cell's own genes take the cell apart at the right moment, and the emptied cell then works for the tree for years.
deep_truth.evidence: In Pipe Maps and in Bark or Wood, the dye travelled only in the xylem, and working xylem pipes are dead cells. A hollow tamarind tree still bears leaves and fruit. Yet a tree whose dead wood is whole dies if one thin ring of living bark is removed.

three.who_am_i: The top layer of your skin, your hair and your nails are dead cells that your body made and keeps for protection. So you, too, are a living body that depends on dead cells.
three.what_is_life: A living body is not alive in every part. Living cells and dead cells work together in a tree, and the tree needs both.
three.what_is_this_world: A wooden door, a page of your notebook and a jute bag are made of cell walls that plants built. Much of what people build with was built first by living cells.

roots.thread: A whole tree grows from one cell, the fertilised egg cell inside a seed. That cell divides, and all the cells that follow carry the same instructions. Yet some become skin, some become packing, some become living phloem, and some die to become xylem. In the cambium, a single thin layer makes wood on one side and bark on the other. So one cell becomes the many tissues of a tree, and the many tissues work as one body.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka shows his son a great tree. If someone cuts the tree at the root, in the middle or at the top, sap runs out, yet the tree lives. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If life leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up.
teachings.link: Uddalaka saw what this unit shows: sap runs through every part of a tree, and one part can die while the rest lives. He used the tree to ask what it is that leaves when a living being dies. Science can describe the pipes and the cells. That question is still open.

teachings.link: A xylem pipe is useful to the tree because the pipe is empty. The cell had to clear out everything inside before water could pass.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply into a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in it. Without them the paper could not be here.
teachings.link: Paper is made from wood, and wood is xylem cells. The page really is made of the pipes that once carried rain water up a tree.

science.text: The death of a xylem cell is switched on by the cell's own genes, at a set stage of growth. Biologists call this programmed cell death.
Every cell of a tree comes from one first cell and carries nearly the same DNA. Cells become different tissues by using different parts of it.
How each new cell beside the cambium comes to be wood or phloem is only partly understood. Signals from neighbouring cells are part of the answer.

other_view.view: A xylem cell does not die 'for' the tree. Its death is a chain of chemical steps set off by its genes, and words like 'job' are our way of telling the story. Some also say the dead wood is not part of the living tree at all. They see it as something the tree has made, as a snail makes a shell.

practice.title: A hand on wood
practice.say: Let's find something made of bare wood, like a door or a table. Put your palm flat on it and close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. Every line you can feel was made by living cells, and each cell built a wall and then died. Water once rose through this wood to leaves in the sun. Now touch your own hair. Those are cells your body made, and they are dead too. They are still part of you.
practice.kid: Find a wooden door or table. Put your palm flat on the wood. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. Living cells built this wood, then died. Now touch your hair. It is made of dead cells too.

ask: Is the dead wood inside a living tree part of the tree, or something the tree made?
Your hair and nails are dead cells. Are they part of you?
A xylem cell works only after dying. Does that make dying a part of living?
